stem:
A 61-year-old man on a medical ward has a right subclavian central venous catheter inserted for intravenous access. Twenty minutes later he becomes acutely distressed and short of breath. His blood pressure has fallen to 78/44 mmHg, his neck veins are distended, the trachea is shifted to the left, and the right side of the chest is hyper-resonant with no audible breath sounds.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Tension pneumothorax
options.B: Cardiac tamponade from vessel perforation
options.C: Massive right haemothorax
options.D: Venous air embolism
options.E: Anaphylaxis to the catheter

correct_answer: A. Tension pneumothorax
why_correct: Hypotension, distended neck veins, tracheal deviation away from the affected side and a hyper-resonant chest with absent breath sounds after a subclavian puncture indicate a tension pneumothorax causing obstructive shock. Pneumothorax is a recognised complication of subclavian and internal jugular line insertion, and the tension form is a clinical diagnosis that needs immediate decompression. Source: BTS Guideline for Pleural Disease, 2023; ATLS (American College of Surgeons), 10th edition.
why_wrong: B. Tamponade also causes hypotension and raised neck veins, but breath sounds are preserved and the trachea stays central. C. A massive haemothorax makes the chest dull to percussion, not hyper-resonant. D. Air embolism can cause sudden collapse but does not produce one-sided hyper-resonance with absent breath sounds. E. Anaphylaxis gives wheeze, rash or swelling with bilateral chest signs, not a silent, hyper-resonant hemithorax.
pearl: Any new breathlessness and hypotension after a central line, pleural procedure or positive-pressure ventilation should make you check for a tension pneumothorax first.
thinking: Procedure near the pleura followed by acute collapse  ↓  Shock with raised neck veins  ↓  Hyper-resonant, silent hemithorax with trachea pushed away  ↓  Tension pneumothorax
exam_trap: Raised neck veins plus hypotension tempts candidates towards tamponade, but percussion note and breath sounds separate the two.
takeaway: Hyper-resonance, absent breath sounds and tracheal shift away from the side in a shocked patient means tension pneumothorax, whatever the cause.
notes: New iatrogenic (post-subclavian line) scenario to avoid duplicating BX389 (post-RTC trauma, same diagnosis) and RES009 (trauma, management). Options rewritten with plausible procedure-related distractors.

stem:
A 47-year-old woman is being mechanically ventilated on the intensive care unit after an emergency laparotomy. Her airway pressures suddenly rise, her oxygen saturation drops to 82% and her blood pressure falls to 70/40 mmHg. Breath sounds are absent on the left, the left chest is hyper-resonant and her neck veins are distended. A portable chest X-ray has been requested.

What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.A: Wait for the portable chest X-ray to confirm the side
options.B: Increase the PEEP to improve her oxygenation
options.C: Decompress the left chest immediately
options.D: Arrange an urgent CT scan of the chest
options.E: Send an arterial blood gas and then reassess

correct_answer: C. Decompress the left chest immediately
why_correct: Rising airway pressures, hypoxia, hypotension and a silent, hyper-resonant left chest in a ventilated patient indicate a tension pneumothorax, which is a clinical diagnosis. Positive-pressure ventilation drives more air into the pleural space, so decompression (finger thoracostomy is usual in a ventilated patient, or needle decompression) must happen at once, followed by a chest drain, without waiting for imaging. Source: BTS Guideline for Pleural Disease, 2023; ATLS (American College of Surgeons), 10th edition.
why_wrong: A. Waiting for an X-ray allows progression to cardiac arrest in a patient who already has obstructive shock. B. Raising PEEP increases intrathoracic pressure and will worsen the tension and the hypotension. D. Moving a shocked, ventilated patient to CT delays life-saving treatment and is unsafe. E. A blood gas will not change the need for decompression and only delays it.
pearl: Positive-pressure ventilation can turn a small pneumothorax into a tension pneumothorax within minutes, so a sudden rise in airway pressure with hypotension demands a chest examination.
thinking: Ventilated patient with sudden high airway pressures  ↓  Hypotension and hypoxia  ↓  Unilateral silent, hyper-resonant chest  ↓  Tension pneumothorax: decompress now, imaging later
exam_trap: The X-ray has already been requested, and candidates feel they should wait for it, but imaging is never required before decompressing a clinically obvious tension pneumothorax.
takeaway: Treat a clinically suspected tension pneumothorax with immediate decompression, not with imaging or ventilator adjustments.
notes: New ICU/ventilated scenario so it differs from RES009 (trauma, decompress before imaging) and from PAN1273 (spontaneous pneumothorax in ED), which teach the same principle. Distractor about PEEP added as a ventilation-specific trap.

stem:
A 76-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes treated with gliclazide was admitted with a urinary tract infection and has been eating very little. On the morning ward round she cannot be roused and does not respond to voice. Her capillary glucose is 1.9 mmol/L. She has a working intravenous cannula in her forearm.

What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Squeeze glucose gel into her cheek and recheck in 15 minutes
options.B: Sit her up and give a sugary drink through a straw
options.C: Give intravenous glucose through the cannula
options.D: Send a laboratory glucose and treat once it is confirmed
options.E: Give dextrose tablets crushed in a little water

correct_answer: C. Give intravenous glucose through the cannula
why_correct: A patient with hypoglycaemia who is unconscious or cannot swallow safely needs parenteral treatment, and with IV access already in place intravenous glucose is the treatment of choice; IM glucagon is used only if IV access cannot be obtained and may work less well in sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia. The capillary glucose is rechecked shortly afterwards, followed by longer-acting carbohydrate once she can eat, and close monitoring because gliclazide-related hypoglycaemia can recur. Source: JBDS-IP, The Hospital Management of Hypoglycaemia in Adults with Diabetes Mellitus, 2022.
why_wrong: A. Buccal gel is not appropriate when the patient is unconscious because of aspiration risk and unreliable absorption. B. Giving a drink to an unrousable patient risks aspiration. D. Severe hypoglycaemia can cause seizures and brain injury, so treatment must not wait for a laboratory result. E. Oral tablets, even crushed, cannot be swallowed safely by an unconscious patient.
pearl: Hypoglycaemia caused by a sulfonylurea such as gliclazide can be prolonged, so the patient needs repeated glucose checks after the initial recovery.
thinking: Unrousable patient with low capillary glucose  ↓  Cannot swallow safely, so no oral or buccal route  ↓  IV access available  ↓  Give IV glucose, then recheck and monitor
exam_trap: Glucose gel feels like the safe first step, but anything placed in the mouth of an unconscious patient risks aspiration.
takeaway: Unconscious hypoglycaemia needs parenteral treatment: IV glucose if there is access, IM glucagon only if there is not.
notes: Angle changed to a ward patient with an existing cannula (key = IV glucose) to avoid duplicating END010 (no IV access, key = IM glucagon). Added the sulfonylurea recurrence and reduced glucagon effectiveness points. Dose and concentration of glucose deliberately omitted (movable figures).

stem:
A 58-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with a three-day history of fever and a productive cough. The team suspects pneumonia. His observations give a NEWS2 score of 9.

Using current NICE sepsis guidance, how should this score be interpreted?

options.A: Medium risk, so repeat the score within the next hour
options.B: Low risk, provided that he is alert and talking
options.C: Confirmed septic shock needing vasopressor support
options.D: It cannot be interpreted until the lactate is known
options.E: High risk of severe illness or death from sepsis

correct_answer: E. High risk of severe illness or death from sepsis
why_correct: In people aged 16 or over with suspected infection, NICE uses NEWS2 to grade risk, and a score of 7 or more suggests a high risk of severe illness or death from sepsis. A high-risk patient needs urgent assessment by a clinician at FY2 level or above, referral to a senior clinical decision maker as soon as possible, and broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour, with the score always interpreted alongside clinical judgement. Source: NICE NG253, Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over, 2025 (updated 2026).
why_wrong: A. Medium risk corresponds to a score of 5 or 6, not a score as high as this. B. Being alert does not lower the risk once the aggregate score is this high. C. NEWS2 grades risk; it does not diagnose septic shock, which needs persistent hypotension needing vasopressors. D. The NEWS2 score is interpreted at the bedside straight away and does not depend on blood results.
pearl: NEWS2 is a bedside score of physiology, so it can be acted on immediately without waiting for any blood test.
thinking: Suspected infection  ↓  Calculate NEWS2  ↓  Score well into the top band  ↓  High risk: senior review and IV antibiotics now
exam_trap: Candidates sometimes think a patient who is talking cannot be high risk, but the aggregate physiology score takes priority.
takeaway: In suspected sepsis, a high NEWS2 score means high risk and triggers immediate senior review and treatment.
notes: Score set at 9 (clearly in the top band) rather than 7, so the key does not hinge on the exact cut-off; the NEWS2 bands are kept as core UK escalation figures PLAB relies on. Reviewer: the 7/5-6 cut-offs appear only in the explanation. PAN1399 (same learning point) is skipped as a within-batch duplicate.

stem:
In an outpatient clinic waiting area, a 66-year-old man slumps forward in his chair and slides to the floor. He does not respond when you shout and gently shake his shoulders. You open his airway and, over the next few seconds, he makes only occasional noisy, gasping breaths.

What is the most appropriate next action?

options.A: Call the arrest team and start chest compressions
options.B: Roll him into the recovery position and watch his breathing
options.C: Feel for a carotid pulse for a full minute before acting
options.D: Give five rescue breaths, then reassess for two minutes
options.E: Fetch a pulse oximeter to confirm his oxygen saturation

correct_answer: A. Call the arrest team and start chest compressions
why_correct: A person who is unresponsive and not breathing normally is in cardiac arrest until proven otherwise; occasional gasps (agonal breathing) are a sign of arrest, not of adequate breathing. Help should be summoned (in UK hospitals, the 2222 arrest call), chest compressions started immediately, and a defibrillator brought, spending no more than 10 seconds assessing breathing. Source: Resuscitation Council UK Guidelines, 2025.
why_wrong: B. The recovery position is for unresponsive people who are breathing normally, not for someone in cardiac arrest. C. A prolonged pulse check delays compressions; assessment should take no more than a few seconds. D. Adult resuscitation starts with chest compressions, and pausing to reassess for minutes is wrong. E. Waiting for monitoring delays CPR, and pulse oximetry is unreliable in cardiac arrest.
pearl: Agonal gasping is common in the first minutes after cardiac arrest and is often mistaken for breathing.
thinking: Unresponsive  ↓  Not breathing normally (gasps only)  ↓  Treat as cardiac arrest  ↓  Call for help and start compressions, get a defibrillator
exam_trap: Noisy gasps can make candidates choose the recovery position, but gasping is not normal breathing.
takeaway: Unresponsive with absent or abnormal breathing means start CPR and call for help immediately.
notes: New in-hospital clinic scenario with explicit agonal gasping as the discriminator. Updated citation to RCUK 2025 guidelines (principles unchanged from 2021). Distinct from ACU006 (choking leading to arrest).

stem:
You are an off-duty doctor at a railway station giving chest compressions to a 52-year-old woman who collapsed and is not breathing normally. A member of station staff runs over with the station's public-access defibrillator.

What is the most appropriate way to use it?

options.A: Complete two full minutes of compressions before opening it
options.B: Turn it on, attach the pads and follow its voice prompts
options.C: Stop all compressions while the pads go on and it charges
options.D: Check for a pulse before deciding whether to attach pads
options.E: Keep it unopened until paramedics can interpret the rhythm

correct_answer: B. Turn it on, attach the pads and follow its voice prompts
why_correct: An automated external defibrillator (AED) should be switched on and attached as soon as it arrives, with its spoken instructions followed. Compressions continue while the pads are applied (by a second rescuer if available), and pauses are kept as short as possible for rhythm analysis and any shock, because early defibrillation of a shockable rhythm is the main determinant of survival. Source: Resuscitation Council UK Guidelines, 2025.
why_wrong: A. Delaying attachment postpones defibrillation, and survival falls with every minute of delay. C. Compressions should continue while the pads are placed, with interruptions kept to a minimum. D. A pulse check delays rhythm analysis and is unreliable; the AED will assess the rhythm. E. Public-access AEDs are designed for anyone to use, and waiting for paramedics loses vital minutes.
pearl: Public-access AEDs analyse the rhythm themselves and will only allow a shock when a shockable rhythm is detected.
thinking: Cardiac arrest with CPR in progress  ↓  AED arrives  ↓  Switch on and attach pads while compressions continue  ↓  Follow prompts, minimise pauses, stand clear for the shock
exam_trap: Some candidates think the cycle of CPR must be completed first, but the AED is attached as soon as it is available.
takeaway: Attach an AED as soon as it arrives and follow its prompts, keeping interruptions to compressions minimal.
notes: New out-of-hospital scenario (off-duty doctor, station AED). Options reordered and reworded. Citation updated to RCUK 2025.

stem:
A 19-year-old student is carried into the emergency department waiting room by friends after drinking heavily at a party. He does not respond to voice, but he is breathing normally at a regular rate, has a strong radial pulse and there is no history of a fall or other injury. Staff are fetching a trolley.

What is the most appropriate immediate step?

options.A: Start chest compressions in case he is about to arrest
options.B: Sit him upright in a chair so that his airway stays clear
options.C: Give abdominal thrusts to clear any airway obstruction
options.D: Recovery position, monitor his breathing, get help
options.E: Lay him flat on his back and leave him to sleep it off

correct_answer: D. Recovery position, monitor his breathing, get help
why_correct: An unresponsive person who is breathing normally, with no suspected spinal injury, should be placed in the recovery position to keep the airway open and let vomit drain, with help summoned and breathing checked continually. If breathing becomes abnormal or stops, CPR should be started straight away; his capillary glucose should also be checked, because alcohol can cause hypoglycaemia. Source: Resuscitation Council UK Guidelines, 2025.
why_wrong: A. Chest compressions are harmful and not indicated in someone who is breathing normally with a pulse. B. An unconscious person propped upright can lose their airway and fall. C. Abdominal thrusts are for a conscious adult with severe choking, not for an unconscious person who is breathing normally. E. Lying supine allows the tongue to obstruct the airway and vomit to be aspirated, and he must not be left unattended.
pearl: Intoxicated, unresponsive patients are at high risk of aspirating vomit, which is why the recovery position matters.
thinking: Unresponsive  ↓  Breathing normally with a pulse  ↓  No suspected spinal injury  ↓  Recovery position, call for help, keep reassessing
exam_trap: Candidates sometimes leave an intoxicated patient lying on his back to 'sleep it off', which risks airway obstruction and aspiration.
takeaway: An unconscious patient who is breathing normally goes into the recovery position with continual monitoring.
notes: New alcohol-intoxication scenario. Added safety point to check capillary glucose. Citation updated to RCUK 2025.

presentation: Anaphylaxis not responding to first adrenaline
stem:
A 31-year-old woman develops lip swelling, wheeze and a hoarse voice minutes after eating a dessert containing cashew nuts, and is brought straight into the emergency department. She is given IM adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh, high-flow oxygen and an IV fluid bolus. Five minutes later she still has stridor and widespread wheeze, and her blood pressure remains 80/45 mmHg.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Give IV chlorphenamine and hydrocortisone and observe her
options.B: Give a rapid 1 mg IV adrenaline bolus
options.C: Nebulise salbutamol and reassess her in an hour
options.D: Wait, as the first dose may still be taking effect
options.E: Repeat IM adrenaline and call for critical care help

correct_answer: E. Repeat IM adrenaline and call for critical care help
why_correct: If airway, breathing or circulation problems persist five minutes after the first IM adrenaline dose, the dose is repeated while oxygen and IV fluids continue. Persisting problems after two IM doses define refractory anaphylaxis, which needs urgent critical care input and an IV adrenaline infusion given by experienced clinicians. Source: Resuscitation Council UK, Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis, 2021.
why_wrong: A. Antihistamines and steroids do not treat airway or circulatory compromise and are not part of the immediate treatment of anaphylaxis. B. A 1 mg IV bolus is the cardiac arrest dose and can cause dangerous arrhythmias and hypertension in a patient with a pulse. C. Salbutamol may help wheeze but does not treat stridor or shock, and waiting an hour risks deterioration. D. Ongoing stridor and hypotension at five minutes mean the first dose has not worked and another is needed now.
pearl: Two IM adrenaline doses without improvement define refractory anaphylaxis, which needs an adrenaline infusion under critical care.
thinking: Anaphylaxis treated with IM adrenaline  ↓  Still stridor and hypotension at five minutes  ↓  Repeat IM adrenaline, continue oxygen and fluids  ↓  Call critical care in case it is refractory
exam_trap: Reaching for antihistamines and steroids feels like 'doing more', but only adrenaline treats the life-threatening features.
takeaway: Persistent anaphylaxis after the first dose needs repeat IM adrenaline and early critical care involvement.
notes: Re-angled so the key does not hinge on recalling the 5-minute repeat interval: the elapsed time is given in the stem and the 30-minute distractor removed. Adrenaline dose bands omitted. IV bolus distractor now explains the danger.

stem:
On the fifth day after a total hip replacement, a 71-year-old woman suddenly becomes breathless and light-headed while walking to the bathroom. She is pale and sweaty, with a heart rate of 128/min, a blood pressure of 74/42 mmHg despite an initial fluid bolus, a raised jugular venous pressure and a clear chest. Her oxygen saturation is 88% on room air.

What is the most appropriate management approach?

options.A: Manage as high-risk PE with urgent senior input
options.B: Send a D-dimer and arrange CTPA only if it is raised
options.C: Book a CT pulmonary angiogram for the next routine list
options.D: Start oral apixaban and review her on tomorrow's round
options.E: Give further fluid boluses until her pressure normalises

correct_answer: A. Manage as high-risk PE with urgent senior input
why_correct: Suspected pulmonary embolism with hypotension is high-risk (massive) PE with a high early mortality, so the stable-patient pathway is bypassed. She needs immediate resuscitation, anticoagulation (usually unfractionated heparin), and urgent senior or critical care input to consider thrombolysis, with bedside echocardiography if she is too unstable for CT pulmonary angiography. Source: NICE NG158, Venous thromboembolic diseases, 2020; ESC Guidelines on acute pulmonary embolism, 2019.
why_wrong: B. D-dimer is a rule-out test for haemodynamically stable patients and only delays treatment here. C. A routine scan list is far too slow for a shocked patient who may need thrombolysis. D. Oral anticoagulation with next-day review is unsafe in a haemodynamically unstable patient. E. Large-volume fluid can overload a failing right ventricle and does not treat the obstruction.
pearl: In high-risk PE the right ventricle is failing against an obstruction, so cautious fluids and early reperfusion matter more than repeated boluses.
thinking: Post-operative patient with sudden breathlessness  ↓  Hypotension, raised JVP, clear chest  ↓  Suspected PE with shock = high risk  ↓  Resuscitate, anticoagulate, urgent senior input for thrombolysis
exam_trap: Candidates follow the stable PE pathway (Wells score, D-dimer) even when the patient is shocked.
takeaway: Suspected PE with shock is high-risk PE and needs immediate resuscitation and specialist input, not the routine diagnostic pathway.
notes: New post-arthroplasty scenario. Overlaps in learning point with PAN1412 (same batch) and BX265 (labelling, not management); scenarios differ, but a reviewer may wish to retire one of PAN1271/PAN1412. Added the over-filling distractor.

stem:
A 23-year-old tall, thin man comes to the emergency department with sudden left-sided chest pain and breathlessness that began while he was resting. While waiting for imaging he becomes agitated and cyanosed, with a heart rate of 140/min, a blood pressure of 76/40 mmHg, a trachea deviated to the right and no breath sounds on the left.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Give high-flow oxygen and await re-expansion of the lung
options.B: Decompress the chest before any imaging is done
options.C: Obtain an urgent chest X-ray to confirm the side first
options.D: Arrange a CT thorax to look for bullous lung disease
options.E: Intubate him and start positive pressure ventilation

correct_answer: B. Decompress the chest before any imaging is done
why_correct: A primary spontaneous pneumothorax has progressed to a tension pneumothorax, shown by hypotension, tracheal deviation away from the affected side and absent breath sounds. This is a clinical diagnosis, and immediate decompression by needle or finger thoracostomy, followed by a chest drain, must not be delayed for imaging. Source: BTS Guideline for Pleural Disease, 2023.
why_wrong: A. Oxygen does not relieve the raised intrapleural pressure, and waiting risks cardiac arrest. C. Delaying for an X-ray can allow progression to cardiac arrest from obstructed venous return. D. CT has a role later in looking for underlying lung disease but not in a shocked patient. E. Positive-pressure ventilation before decompression can rapidly worsen a tension pneumothorax.
pearl: Although tension physiology is rarer in spontaneous than in traumatic or ventilated pneumothorax, it can develop in any pneumothorax.
thinking: Young tall man with sudden pleuritic pain  ↓  Develops shock, tracheal shift and a silent hemithorax  ↓  Tension pneumothorax  ↓  Decompress immediately, chest drain after
exam_trap: Because he is already waiting for imaging, candidates feel the X-ray should come first, but deterioration changes the priority.
takeaway: When a pneumothorax causes shock, decompress first and image afterwards.
notes: New spontaneous-pneumothorax scenario in ED, different from RES009 (trauma) and PAN1089 (ventilated ICU patient), which share the learning point. Decompression site figures omitted.

stem:
A 69-year-old man has been on the medical ward for a day receiving IV antibiotics for community-acquired pneumonia. The nurse calls you because over the last hour he has become disorientated and is pulling at his cannula. His respiratory rate has risen to 30/min and his blood pressure has fallen to 84/50 mmHg from 118/70 mmHg on admission.

What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Continue the current plan and review at the next ward round
options.B: Change his observations to four-hourly and recheck later
options.C: Reassess him now and escalate to senior help
options.D: Give oral lorazepam to settle his agitation
options.E: Wait for blood culture sensitivities before changing anything

correct_answer: C. Reassess him now and escalate to senior help
why_correct: New confusion, tachypnoea and falling blood pressure despite antibiotics show that his sepsis is worsening, so his risk is now higher than at his initial assessment. He needs immediate bedside reassessment using an ABCDE approach, review by a senior clinical decision maker and escalation to critical care outreach or intensive care if he does not respond. Source: NICE NG253, Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over, 2024.
why_wrong: A. A plan made before deterioration may no longer be adequate and must be reviewed now. B. Less frequent observations are the opposite of what a deteriorating patient needs. D. Sedation masks worsening confusion and can worsen hypotension and breathing. E. Culture results take days, and waiting for them delays escalation of a deteriorating patient.
pearl: Deterioration after treatment has started should prompt a fresh risk assessment rather than reliance on the original plan.
thinking: Patient on treatment for infection  ↓  New confusion, tachypnoea, hypotension  ↓  Sepsis worsening  ↓  Reassess now and escalate
exam_trap: Agitation tempts candidates to sedate, which hides the deterioration it is caused by.
takeaway: Worsening observations in a patient on treatment for infection need immediate reassessment and escalation.
notes: Dropped at independent check: Within-batch duplicate: vignette (older man with pneumonia on the ward, nurse calls, new confusion, tachypnoea, falling BP, key reassess/escalate) is near-identical to PAN1426, and the learning point is also covered by PAN1404. Adds nothing distinct.

stem:
A 19-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes has had two days of vomiting and abdominal pain and stopped taking her insulin. She is breathing deeply and rapidly. An arterial blood gas on room air shows:

- pH 7.21
- PaCO₂ 3.1 kPa
- HCO₃⁻ 11 mmol/L

Which acid–base disturbance is shown?

options.A: Respiratory alkalosis with metabolic compensation
options.B: Respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation
options.C: Mixed metabolic and respiratory acidosis
options.D: Metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation
options.E: Metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation

correct_answer: E. Metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation
why_correct: The low pH shows acidaemia and the low bicarbonate shows that the primary process is metabolic, consistent with diabetic ketoacidosis. The low PaCO₂ reflects deep, rapid (Kussmaul) breathing that partly compensates, and it is roughly what would be expected for this degree of acidosis, so there is no separate respiratory problem. Source: JBDS-IP, The Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults, 2023.
why_wrong: A. In a respiratory alkalosis the pH would be raised, not low. B. A respiratory acidosis needs a raised PaCO₂, whereas here it is low. C. A mixed acidosis would show a raised or inappropriately normal PaCO₂, not a low one. D. A metabolic alkalosis would give a high pH and a raised bicarbonate.
pearl: Compensation never fully corrects the pH, so the direction of the pH tells you the primary disturbance.
thinking: pH low: acidaemia  ↓  Bicarbonate low: metabolic cause  ↓  PaCO₂ low in the same direction: compensation  ↓  Metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation
exam_trap: Seeing a low PaCO₂, candidates jump to a respiratory alkalosis without first checking whether the pH is high or low.
takeaway: Read the pH first, then match the parameter that explains it; the other moving in the same direction is compensation.
notes: New DKA vignette with different ABG values (Winter's check: expected PaCO₂ about 3.0-3.5 kPa, so 3.1 is appropriate). The Winter's formula figure is omitted from the explanation (deep reference figure).

presentation: Fever and shock after bowel surgery
stem:
Three days after a bowel resection, a 63-year-old woman on the surgical ward has worsening abdominal pain and a temperature of 38.4°C. Over the afternoon her heart rate climbs to 125/min, her blood pressure falls to 88/54 mmHg and she becomes newly confused about where she is.

What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Recognise possible sepsis and escalate to a senior now
options.B: Encourage oral fluids and repeat observations in four hours
options.C: Give haloperidol for confusion and review on the ward round
options.D: Continue current care, as post-operative fever is expected
options.E: Increase observations to hourly and hand over to the night team

correct_answer: A. Recognise possible sepsis and escalate to a senior now
why_correct: Tachycardia, hypotension and new confusion with fever after bowel surgery suggest sepsis, possibly from an anastomotic leak, and these are high-risk features. She needs immediate review by a senior clinical decision maker, IV fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics without delay, and early involvement of the surgical team to find and control the source. Source: NICE NG253, Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over, 2024.
why_wrong: B. Oral fluids and delayed observations are inadequate for hypotension from possible septic shock. C. Sedation masks deterioration, can worsen hypotension and delays escalation. D. Fever with shock and confusion is not an expected post-operative finding and must be investigated. E. Waiting to hand over delays time-critical treatment and source control.
pearl: Recent surgery is a recognised risk factor for sepsis, and source control such as drainage or re-operation may be needed as well as antibiotics.
thinking: Recent abdominal surgery  ↓  Fever, tachycardia, hypotension, new confusion  ↓  Suspected sepsis, possible anastomotic leak  ↓  Escalate to a senior now, treat and seek the source
exam_trap: Fever after surgery is often dismissed as 'normal', but with shock and confusion it signals sepsis.
takeaway: New confusion with hypotension and tachycardia in a patient with infection is high-risk sepsis needing immediate escalation.
notes: Dropped at independent check: Duplicates live GF040 (day 3 after bowel resection, new confusion and tachypnoea, key escalate to registrar/outreach) and ACU007 (post-op deterioration with new confusion, escalate to senior) in both scenario and learning point; also overlaps the in-batch escalating-sepsis cluster (PAN1404/PAN1426/PAN205).

stem:
A 66-year-old man who takes naproxen for knee osteoarthritis vomits a large amount of fresh red blood at home and is brought to the emergency department. He looks pale and sweaty, his heart rate is 122/min and his blood pressure is 94/58 mmHg. A full blood count has been sent.

What should be done first?

options.A: Arrange an outpatient endoscopy within the next two weeks
options.B: Assess and resuscitate him using an ABCDE approach
options.C: Start oral omeprazole and review when bloods are back
options.D: Request a CT abdomen before any resuscitation
options.E: Wait for the haemoglobin result to judge blood loss

correct_answer: B. Assess and resuscitate him using an ABCDE approach
why_correct: Haematemesis with pallor, tachycardia and low blood pressure indicates a significant upper gastrointestinal bleed with shock, so ABCDE assessment and resuscitation come first, including large-bore IV access, bloods with crossmatch and blood products as needed. Once resuscitated he should have risk scoring and endoscopy immediately after resuscitation because he is unstable. Source: NICE CG141, Acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding in over 16s, 2012 (updated 2016).
why_wrong: A. An unstable patient with active bleeding needs inpatient endoscopy after resuscitation, not outpatient investigation. C. NICE advises against starting acid suppression before endoscopy, and delaying assessment is unsafe. D. Resuscitation must come before imaging, and endoscopy is the investigation of choice. E. The haemoglobin may not have fallen yet in acute bleeding, so it cannot be used to delay resuscitation.
pearl: In acute bleeding the haemoglobin can be near normal at first because whole blood is lost; heart rate and blood pressure are better early guides.
thinking: Haematemesis on an NSAID  ↓  Pale, tachycardic, hypotensive  ↓  Shocked upper GI bleed  ↓  ABCDE resuscitation first, then endoscopy
exam_trap: A normal early haemoglobin falsely reassures candidates that the bleed is small.
takeaway: In a shocked upper GI bleed, resuscitate first and arrange endoscopy once the patient is stabilised.
notes: New NSAID-related bleed scenario. Changed the PPI distractor to oral omeprazole and explained that CG141 advises against acid suppression before endoscopy. Distinct from GAS043 (variceal bleed, terlipressin).

stem:
A 34-year-old cyclist who was not wearing a helmet is brought to the emergency department after falling from his bike and striking his head on the kerb. Since arrival he has vomited three times, and he is becoming harder to rouse, now opening his eyes only to voice.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Discharge with written head injury advice and a responsible adult
options.B: Arrange a skull X-ray to look for a fracture
options.C: Admit for overnight neurological observations without imaging
options.D: Request an urgent CT head scan
options.E: Give an antiemetic and review him in the morning

correct_answer: D. Request an urgent CT head scan
why_correct: Repeated vomiting and a falling level of consciousness after head injury are features of a possible intracranial injury, and NICE recommends a CT head scan within 1 hour for adults with these features. A falling GCS also needs airway assessment, senior input and early discussion with neurosurgery if a bleed is found. Source: NICE NG232, Head injury: assessment and early management, 2023.
why_wrong: A. Discharge with red-flag features risks missing an expanding intracranial haematoma. B. A skull X-ray cannot exclude intracranial bleeding and is not recommended. C. Observation without imaging delays diagnosis of a treatable bleed. E. An antiemetic treats the symptom but not the cause, and waiting until morning is dangerous.
pearl: A falling GCS after head injury is more worrying than any single GCS value, and needs repeated recording.
thinking: Head injury  ↓  Repeated vomiting and falling consciousness  ↓  Possible intracranial haematoma  ↓  Urgent CT head and senior review
exam_trap: Admitting for observation feels cautious, but in the presence of red flags imaging must not be delayed.
takeaway: Repeated vomiting or a deteriorating conscious level after head injury needs an urgent CT head scan.
notes: New adult cyclist scenario. Replaced weak distractors (sleeping tablet, return in weeks) with plausible ones (skull X-ray, observation without imaging, antiemetic).

presentation: Minor head injury on an anticoagulant
stem:
An 82-year-old woman who takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation trips on a rug at home and bumps her forehead. She did not lose consciousness, has not vomited, and has a GCS of 15 with no neurological deficit. She lives alone and is keen to go home.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Discharge with written advice, as she appears well
options.B: Send her home and scan only if she starts vomiting
options.C: Withhold tonight's apixaban and refer to the falls clinic
options.D: Arrange a skull X-ray before discharge
options.E: Arrange a CT head scan before deciding on discharge

correct_answer: E. Arrange a CT head scan before deciding on discharge
why_correct: Patients taking anticoagulants (including DOACs such as apixaban) have a higher risk of intracranial haemorrhage after head injury, which may present late. NICE advises considering a CT head scan within 8 hours of the injury even with no other indication, particularly when the person might not be able to return if they deteriorate, as here because she lives alone. Source: NICE NG232, Head injury: assessment and early management, 2023.
why_wrong: A. Appearing well does not exclude a developing bleed in an anticoagulated patient. B. Waiting for symptoms risks a delayed diagnosis of an expanding haematoma, and she lives alone. C. Withholding a dose does not exclude a bleed that may already be present. D. A skull X-ray cannot exclude intracranial haemorrhage and is not recommended.
pearl: If a traumatic intracranial bleed is found, the anticoagulant may need urgent reversal on specialist advice.
thinking: Head injury  ↓  Taking an anticoagulant  ↓  Higher, possibly delayed, bleeding risk  ↓  CT head even if she looks well
exam_trap: A well-looking patient with a normal GCS tempts candidates to discharge without imaging.
takeaway: Anticoagulated patients with head injury should be considered for CT even when they appear well.
notes: New vignette (apixaban, lives alone). Wording matched to NG232 1.5.13, which says 'consider' CT within 8 hours, with the example of a person who might not return; the vignette was built so that example applies. No loss of consciousness or amnesia, so the age-65 criterion does not apply.

SKIP: duplicates PAN1188 in this same batch (both AKT sources N1188 and N1399 teach 'suspected infection with NEWS2 of 7 or more = high risk of severe illness or death from sepsis'), and the item's key rests entirely on recalling the NEWS2 cut-off. PAN1188 has been re-angled (score of 9) to cover the learning point. Recommend retiring UN1399 rather than replacing it. Source statement itself verified correct against NG253 rec 1.6.2.

stem:
A 73-year-old man with redness and swelling spreading up his left leg is assessed in the emergency department. His respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, blood pressure, pulse, temperature and level of consciousness are all within normal limits, giving a NEWS2 score of 0. However, his skin looks mottled over the knees and his face appears ashen.

How should his risk be judged?

options.A: Very low risk, so routine observations will suffice
options.B: Higher risk than his NEWS2 score alone suggests
options.C: Sepsis is excluded while the NEWS2 score stays at 0
options.D: Mottling is an expected finding at his age
options.E: Low risk until a raised lactate confirms otherwise

correct_answer: B. Higher risk than his NEWS2 score alone suggests
why_correct: NEWS2 supports clinical judgement but does not replace it. NICE advises considering a person's risk as higher than their NEWS2 score suggests if they have a mottled or ashen appearance, a non-blanching rash or cyanosis, so this man needs prompt senior assessment despite normal observations. Source: NICE NG253, Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over, 2025 (updated 2026) (recommendation 1.6.3).
why_wrong: A. Mottled or ashen skin is a warning sign that overrides a reassuring score. C. No NEWS2 score excludes sepsis, especially with concerning clinical signs. D. Mottling reflects poor skin perfusion and is not a normal finding at any age. E. Risk is judged clinically and should not wait for a lactate result.
pearl: Mottled or ashen skin, a non-blanching rash and cyanosis are the three appearances NICE singles out as raising risk above the NEWS2 score.
thinking: Suspected infection  ↓  NEWS2 of 0  ↓  Mottled, ashen appearance  ↓  Treat as higher risk than the score suggests
exam_trap: Candidates trust a score of 0 and ignore what they see at the bedside.
takeaway: Clinical signs of poor perfusion can make a patient higher risk than a low NEWS2 score suggests.
notes: New cellulitis vignette. Recommendation number checked against current NG253 (1.6.3).

stem:
A 46-year-old woman admitted with pyelonephritis has her observations recorded on the ward. Her pulse, blood pressure, temperature, oxygen saturation and alertness all score 0, but her respiratory rate of 26/min scores 3, giving a total NEWS2 score of 3.

According to NICE sepsis guidance, what is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Continue routine observations because her total score is low
options.B: Repeat the score in an hour and escalate only if it reaches 5
options.C: Ask for a high-priority review by an FY2 doctor or above
options.D: Start oral antibiotics and continue routine observations
options.E: Transfer her straight to intensive care for organ support

correct_answer: C. Ask for a high-priority review by an FY2 doctor or above
why_correct: In suspected sepsis, NICE advises that when a single parameter contributes 3 points to the NEWS2 score, a high-priority review should be requested from a clinician with core competencies in acutely ill patients (FY2, a second-year foundation doctor, or above), even when the total is low. That clinician decides whether the abnormal parameter is due to the infection and therefore what the true risk is. Source: NICE NG253, Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over, 2025 (updated 2026).
why_wrong: A. A single parameter scoring 3 is a trigger for review whatever the total. B. Waiting for the total to rise could allow deterioration in a patient who may have sepsis. D. Starting treatment without the review misses the escalation trigger and the risk decision. E. Intensive care may be needed later, but the first step is a prompt medical review to grade her risk.
pearl: A very abnormal single observation can signal organ dysfunction even when the rest of the observations are normal.
thinking: Suspected infection  ↓  Low total NEWS2  ↓  One parameter scores 3  ↓  High-priority review by FY2 or above
exam_trap: Candidates look only at the total score and miss the single-parameter trigger.
takeaway: In suspected sepsis, one NEWS2 parameter scoring 3 needs a high-priority medical review even if the total is low.
notes: New pyelonephritis vignette with the scoring stated in the stem, so the key tests the single-parameter principle rather than recall of NEWS2 respiratory-rate bands. Checked against current NG253 rec 1.6.2.

SKIP (rule 2): the correct answer hinges purely on recalling the NG253 rec 1.6.5 NEWS2 recalculation interval for high-risk patients (every 30 minutes; hourly for medium, 4-6 hourly for low risk, from the AoMRC 2022 statement), a movable monitoring figure. It cannot be re-angled without the options becoming the intervals themselves. Source key verified as currently correct, so the live item is accurate but out of scope for the PLAB rules.

stem:
A 54-year-old man with cellulitis of the lower leg was started on IV antibiotics and given a fluid bolus in the emergency department two hours ago. On the acute medical unit his blood pressure is now lower than on arrival despite the fluid, his skin is cold and clammy, and he has become drowsy and slow to answer questions.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Urgently reassess him and escalate to critical care
options.B: Wait until the next scheduled NEWS2 calculation
options.C: Switch to an oral antibiotic with a broader spectrum
options.D: Treat the drowsiness as delirium and give haloperidol
options.E: Continue the current antibiotics and review in four hours

correct_answer: A. Urgently reassess him and escalate to critical care
why_correct: Worsening hypotension and reduced consciousness despite antibiotics and fluid suggest progression to septic shock, so his risk is now higher than at his first assessment. He needs urgent senior reassessment, review of the source (including the possibility of a necrotising soft-tissue infection) and escalation to critical care for organ support such as vasopressors. Source: NICE NG253, Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over, 2025 (updated 2026).
why_wrong: B. Clinical deterioration demands immediate action, not the next scheduled score. C. Changing to oral therapy is inappropriate in a patient with worsening shock. D. Drowsiness with hypotension suggests poor brain perfusion, and sedation could be harmful. E. A plan made before deterioration is no longer adequate and must be reviewed now.
pearl: Hypotension that persists after a fluid bolus in sepsis suggests septic shock and the likely need for vasopressors.
thinking: Sepsis on treatment  ↓  Lower blood pressure despite fluid, new drowsiness  ↓  Possible septic shock  ↓  Urgent reassessment and critical care referral
exam_trap: Candidates assume treatment already given is enough and wait for the next routine review.
takeaway: Deterioration despite initial sepsis treatment needs urgent reassessment and escalation to critical care.
notes: New cellulitis scenario angled on failure to respond to fluid (septic shock). Same learning point as PAN1274 and PAN1324 in this batch; reviewer may wish to retire one.

stem:
A 38-year-old woman who takes the combined oral contraceptive pill and returned from a long-haul flight two days ago is brought in by ambulance after collapsing at home. She is breathless and clammy, with a heart rate of 135/min and a blood pressure of 72/38 mmHg. Her right calf is swollen and tender, and her ECG shows sinus tachycardia.

What is the immediate priority?

options.A: Calculate a two-level Wells score and await a D-dimer
options.B: Start LMWH and request a CTPA within 24 hours
options.C: Resuscitate and treat as suspected high-risk PE
options.D: Give apixaban and arrange an outpatient leg scan
options.E: Refer her to the ambulatory PE clinic for tomorrow

correct_answer: C. Resuscitate and treat as suspected high-risk PE
why_correct: Collapse and hypotension with a likely source of venous thrombosis indicate suspected high-risk (massive) PE, so the stable-patient pathway of Wells score and D-dimer does not apply. She needs immediate resuscitation, anticoagulation with unfractionated heparin and urgent senior input to consider thrombolysis, with bedside echocardiography if she is too unstable for CT pulmonary angiography. Source: NICE NG158, Venous thromboembolic diseases, 2020; ESC Guidelines on acute pulmonary embolism, 2019.
why_wrong: A. Wells scoring and D-dimer are for haemodynamically stable patients and would delay treatment. B. Delayed imaging is far too slow for a shocked patient who may need thrombolysis. D. Outpatient investigation is unsafe in a shocked patient. E. Ambulatory care is only for stable, low-risk patients.
pearl: Thrombolysis is considered for PE with haemodynamic instability, which is why early senior involvement matters.
thinking: Risk factors for VTE and a swollen calf  ↓  Collapse with hypotension  ↓  Suspected high-risk PE  ↓  Resuscitate, anticoagulate and seek urgent senior input
exam_trap: Candidates apply the familiar Wells and D-dimer steps even when the patient is shocked.
takeaway: In suspected PE with shock, resuscitate and manage as high-risk PE rather than following the stable pathway.
notes: Dropped at independent check: Within-batch duplicate: same learning point and key as PAN1271 (manage as high-risk PE) and a scenario (COCP, long-haul flight, swollen calf, collapse) near-identical to PAN207. Distractors (A,B,D,E all variations of delay) also weaker than PAN1271.

presentation: Afebrile older person with possible sepsis
stem:
An 86-year-old care-home resident is sent in because staff say she 'is just not herself': she has stopped eating, is sleepier than usual and has new urinary incontinence. Her tympanic temperature is 36.4°C. She looks grey and says she feels dreadful.

What is the most accurate interpretation?

options.A: Sepsis is unlikely because she has no fever at all
options.B: Her symptoms suggest a viral illness rather than sepsis
options.C: A normal temperature does not rule out sepsis
options.D: Antibiotics should be withheld until a fever develops
options.E: Her behaviour change is most likely due to ageing

correct_answer: C. A normal temperature does not rule out sepsis
why_correct: People with sepsis, especially older or frail people, often present non-specifically, for example feeling very unwell, and may not have a raised temperature. Concerns from carers about a change from usual behaviour should be taken seriously, and a low temperature can itself be a warning sign. Source: NICE NG253, Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over, 2025 (updated 2026).
why_wrong: A. Absence of fever does not make sepsis unlikely, particularly in older people. B. A normal temperature does not favour a viral cause over sepsis. D. Antibiotic decisions depend on risk assessment and must not wait for a fever. E. An acute change from her usual behaviour needs investigation, not attribution to ageing.
pearl: In older people, reduced eating, new confusion or drowsiness, and new incontinence can be the only clues to sepsis.
thinking: Older care-home resident  ↓  Acute change from usual behaviour and feels very unwell  ↓  Normal temperature  ↓  Sepsis still possible: assess risk now
exam_trap: A normal temperature reassures candidates, but older people often fail to mount a fever.
takeaway: A normal temperature does not exclude sepsis, especially in older people.
notes: New care-home vignette. Added NG253 point about carers' concerns and low temperature as a risk sign.

stem:
A 28-year-old man with a severe learning disability and limited speech is brought to his GP surgery by his support worker. Over two days he has become withdrawn, is refusing food and keeps holding his side. He feels warm to touch but cannot say how he feels.

What is the most appropriate approach to assessing him?

options.A: Rebook him for when a full history can be obtained
options.B: Treat him as low risk unless he reports specific symptoms
options.C: Rely mainly on his own account of how unwell he feels
options.D: Take extra care and ask his carer about changes
options.E: Base the decision on observations alone, not the carer

correct_answer: D. Take extra care and ask his carer about changes
why_correct: People with communication difficulties, such as learning disabilities or cognitive impairment, are at risk of delayed recognition of sepsis, so NICE advises assessing them with extra care. Information from carers about changes from usual behaviour is especially valuable, alongside a structured set of observations. Source: NICE NG253, Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over, 2025 (updated 2026).
why_wrong: A. Delaying assessment risks missing a time-critical illness. B. Communication difficulty increases, not lowers, the risk of missed sepsis. C. He may be unable to convey how unwell he is. E. Observations matter, but carers can give vital information about changes from his baseline.
pearl: Behaviour change, such as withdrawal or refusing food, may be the main sign of illness in someone who cannot describe symptoms.
thinking: Possible infection  ↓  Patient cannot describe symptoms  ↓  Higher risk of delayed recognition  ↓  Extra care, carer's account and structured observations
exam_trap: Candidates treat the absence of reported symptoms as reassurance.
takeaway: Assess people with communication difficulties more carefully for sepsis and use their carers' knowledge.
notes: New GP-surgery vignette with a learning-disability context; wording matched to NG253 rec 1.1.4.

stem:
A 57-year-old woman arrives at the emergency department with rigors, a heart rate of 118/min and a blood pressure of 96/60 mmHg. She is being managed for suspected sepsis and blood cultures have been taken, but no obvious cause has been found yet.

Alongside starting treatment, what else is a priority in her assessment?

options.A: Actively search for the source of infection
options.B: Rely on blood culture results to reveal the source
options.C: Assume a urinary source, as it is the commonest cause
options.D: Delay examination until the antibiotics have taken effect
options.E: Treat empirically as pneumonia without examining her

correct_answer: A. Actively search for the source of infection
why_correct: Finding the likely source of infection through history, examination and targeted tests (for example urine testing and a chest X-ray, with imaging of the abdomen and pelvis if indicated) guides antibiotic choice and identifies infections that need drainage or surgery. NICE advises involving the surgical or interventional radiology team early when a source needs to be controlled. Source: NICE NG253, Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over, 2025 (updated 2026).
why_wrong: B. Blood cultures take time and often grow nothing, so they cannot replace clinical assessment. C. Assuming one source risks missing chest, abdominal, skin or other foci. D. Examination should happen now, alongside treatment, not after it. E. Treating without examining risks missing a source that needs specific treatment or drainage.
pearl: Some sources, such as an abscess or a perforated viscus, will not settle with antibiotics alone and need source control.
thinking: Suspected sepsis  ↓  Start treatment promptly  ↓  Search actively for the source  ↓  Tailor antibiotics and arrange source control
exam_trap: Candidates focus on starting antibiotics and forget that the source may need surgical or radiological control.
takeaway: In sepsis, always look for and control the source as well as starting antibiotics.
notes: New ED vignette; weak distractors (ignore focal symptoms, always pulmonary) replaced with plausible ones. Added source-control point from NG253 1.11.

stem:
A 24-year-old woman attends the emergency department with two days of burning on passing urine and a dull ache in her right flank. She feels tired but is alert, and her respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, blood pressure, pulse, level of consciousness and temperature are all within the normal range, giving a NEWS2 score of 0.

How should this NEWS2 result be interpreted?

options.A: Sepsis has been ruled out, so observations are no longer needed
options.B: Very low risk, but sepsis is not excluded; keep reassessing
options.C: She needs intravenous antibiotics within one hour regardless
options.D: Suspected infection alone means she needs critical care referral
options.E: She can go home without any further clinical assessment

correct_answer: B. Very low risk, but sepsis is not excluded; keep reassessing
why_correct: NICE NG253 states that, in a person with suspected infection, a NEWS2 score of 0 suggests a very low risk of severe illness or death from sepsis, not zero risk. The score must be interpreted alongside history and examination, so she still needs a full clinical assessment of her probable kidney infection, with observations continuing at the standard frequency and re-scoring if her condition changes. Source: NICE NG253, Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over, 2025 (updated 2026).
why_wrong: A. A score of 0 lowers the risk but never rules sepsis out, and observations continue at the routine frequency. C. NG253 links the urgency of antibiotics to the risk level, so a very low-risk patient does not automatically need IV antibiotics within the hour. D. Critical care review is for severe or deteriorating physiology, not for every suspected infection. E. NEWS2 supports but does not replace clinical judgement, and she still needs examination, urine testing and a management plan.
pearl: In suspected infection, NEWS2 grades risk: a score of 0 means very low risk, not 'no sepsis'.
thinking: Suspected infection (probable pyelonephritis)  ↓  NEWS2 0 = very low-risk band  ↓  Score supports, never replaces, clinical judgement  ↓  Full assessment and routine re-scoring; escalate if she changes
exam_trap: Option A is tempting because normal observations feel reassuring, but NICE frames a score of 0 as very low risk rather than exclusion of sepsis.
takeaway: A NEWS2 of 0 means very low risk: keep assessing and keep scoring.
notes: New vignette (young woman with probable pyelonephritis in ED) replacing the bare 'NEWS2 = 0' stem; same learning point and key. Verified against NG253 rec 1.6.2 (score 0 = very low risk) and 1.6.5. Antibiotic-timing rationale for the IV-antibiotics distractor tightened to reflect NG253 risk-based timing.

stem:
A 71-year-old man was admitted with community-acquired pneumonia and started on intravenous antibiotics and fluids. By the next morning his fever had settled and he was eating. On the second evening the nurse calls you because he has become newly muddled, his breathing has quickened and his blood pressure has fallen compared with earlier readings.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Continue the current plan, as he had already responded to treatment
options.B: Reduce observations to four-hourly so he can rest overnight
options.C: Switch to oral antibiotics, as the infection is now improving
options.D: Review him now, repeat NEWS2 and re-grade his sepsis risk
options.E: Ask the day team to review him on tomorrow's ward round

correct_answer: D. Review him now, repeat NEWS2 and re-grade his sepsis risk
why_correct: New confusion, tachypnoea and falling blood pressure after an initial response signal deterioration, which may mean treatment failure, a complication such as empyema, or a new source of infection. NICE NG253 advises recalculating NEWS2 and re-evaluating sepsis risk whenever there is deterioration or an unexpected change, and grading risk higher than the score alone suggests when a patient worsens after interventions. Source: NICE NG253, Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over, 2025 (updated 2026).
why_wrong: A. Earlier improvement does not make a new deterioration safe to ignore; it needs explaining. B. A deteriorating patient needs more frequent, not less frequent, observations. C. Stepping down to oral therapy is inappropriate when he is clinically worsening. E. Deferring review to the next day risks further avoidable deterioration overnight.
pearl: A patient who improves and then worsens is a new emergency: re-score and re-grade rather than relying on the earlier trajectory.
thinking: Pneumonia on IV antibiotics  ↓  Initial improvement  ↓  New confusion, tachypnoea and falling BP  ↓  Bedside reassessment, recalculate NEWS2, re-grade sepsis risk and escalate
exam_trap: Option A tempts candidates who anchor on the earlier response to treatment, but deterioration after improvement may mean treatment failure or a new complication.
takeaway: Deterioration after initial improvement in sepsis demands immediate reassessment and re-stratification of risk.
notes: New vignette (older man with pneumonia on the ward, second evening) replacing the generic stem; options reworded to plausible ward actions. Same learning point and key. Verified against NG253 recs 1.6.4 and 1.6.6.

stem:
An 86-year-old man is on a medical ward being treated for a urinary tract infection. His NEWS2 score this afternoon is low and unchanged from the morning. His daughter tells the nurse he 'is not himself' and is far more muddled than usual, and on examination his knees and hands look mottled and feel cold.

What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Recheck his observations in four hours as the score is low
options.B: Give a night-time sedative to manage the increased confusion
options.C: Continue routine monitoring at the frequency set by the score
options.D: Escalate only if his NEWS2 rises at the next observation round
options.E: Urgent clinical review and escalation despite the low score

correct_answer: E. Urgent clinical review and escalation despite the low score
why_correct: Mottled, cold peripheries and worsening confusion are signs of poor perfusion and possible evolving septic shock, and NEWS2 may not yet reflect them. NICE NG253 advises grading sepsis risk higher than the NEWS2 score suggests when there is mottled or ashen skin or concern about deterioration, so he needs urgent review by a clinician competent in acute care and escalation regardless of the number. Source: NICE NG253, Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over, 2024 (amended 2025).
why_wrong: A. A four-hour delay is unsafe when there are clinical signs of hypoperfusion. B. New confusion may reflect hypoperfusion or sepsis-related delirium, and sedation could mask deterioration and cause harm. C. A low score can be falsely reassuring and must not override clear clinical signs. D. Waiting for the score to rise delays escalation in a patient who is already deteriorating.
pearl: Mottling, new confusion and a relative saying 'he is not himself' are red flags that override a reassuring NEWS2.
thinking: UTI on the ward  ↓  Low, stable NEWS2  ↓  New confusion with mottled, cold peripheries  ↓  Poor perfusion: grade risk higher than the score, review urgently and escalate
exam_trap: Options C and D look protocol-compliant, but NEWS2 is an aid to clinical judgement, not a substitute for it.
takeaway: Clinical signs of deterioration trump a low NEWS2: review and escalate now.
notes: Dropped at independent check: Within-batch duplicate of PAN1400 (low NEWS2 but mottled skin -> risk higher than the score, NG253 1.6.3); also close to live ACU007. Additionally internally inconsistent: new confusion scores 3 on the NEWS2 consciousness parameter, so the score could not be "low and unchanged".

stem:
A 59-year-old woman of African-Caribbean heritage takes lisinopril for hypertension. Over the last hour her lips and tongue have swollen and her voice has become thick and muffled. There is no itch or hives. She is anxious but able to speak.

What is the immediate priority?

options.A: Urgent airway assessment with early senior anaesthetic help
options.B: Oral antihistamine and discharge home if no rash develops
options.C: Stop lisinopril and review her in the GP surgery next week
options.D: Switch lisinopril to an angiotensin II receptor blocker today
options.E: Send a C1-esterase inhibitor level and await the result

correct_answer: A. Urgent airway assessment with early senior anaesthetic help
why_correct: ACE-inhibitor angioedema is bradykinin-mediated, often occurs without urticaria, and tongue swelling with voice change means the upper airway is involved and can obstruct rapidly. The first priority is an ABCDE assessment focused on the airway, with early anaesthetic and ENT involvement so that a definitive airway can be secured if needed; permanent withdrawal of the ACE inhibitor follows. Source: NICE CKS Angio-oedema and anaphylaxis; BNF ACE inhibitors, 2025.
why_wrong: B. Absence of a rash is not reassuring in bradykinin-mediated angioedema, which responds poorly to antihistamines. C. The ACE inhibitor must be stopped, but this does nothing for the immediate airway threat. D. Changing antihypertensive is a later decision, and an ARB is used only with caution after ACE-inhibitor angioedema. E. C1-esterase inhibitor testing can help exclude hereditary or acquired angioedema later but must not delay airway assessment.
pearl: ACE-inhibitor angioedema can occur at any point during treatment, is more common in people of Black African or African-Caribbean origin, and usually lacks urticaria.
thinking: On an ACE inhibitor  ↓  Lip and tongue swelling, no urticaria  ↓  Voice change = upper airway involvement  ↓  Airway first: ABCDE with early senior anaesthetic/ENT help
exam_trap: Option C is the correct long-term step but the wrong immediate priority when the tongue is swelling and the voice is changing.
takeaway: Tongue swelling on an ACE inhibitor is an airway emergency first and a drug reaction second.
notes: New vignette (named drug, voice change, ethnicity risk factor). Same learning point and key (airway first). Near DER006/DER039 test diagnosis and stopping the drug, not the immediate airway priority, so not a duplicate.

stem:
A 74-year-old retired farmer attends the minor injuries unit after a rose thorn and garden soil were driven deep into the palm of his hand while he was clearing a flower bed. The wound has been explored and cleaned. He takes amlodipine and is otherwise well.

Which further assessment is most important to guide his management?

options.A: Thyroid function, calcium and vitamin D levels
options.B: Serum creatine kinase and renal function
options.C: Tetanus immunisation history and wound risk
options.D: Hepatitis A vaccination status
options.E: Blood group and antibody screen

correct_answer: C. Tetanus immunisation history and wound risk
why_correct: A deep, soil-contaminated puncture wound is tetanus-prone, and management depends on both how tetanus-prone the wound is and how many doses of tetanus-containing vaccine he has received; older adults are the group most likely to be incompletely immunised. This decides whether he needs a booster dose and/or human tetanus immunoglobulin alongside thorough wound care. Source: UKHSA Green Book, chapter 30 (Tetanus).
why_wrong: A. Thyroid, calcium and vitamin D levels have no bearing on puncture-wound care. B. Creatine kinase and renal function are relevant to crush or electrical injury, not a thorn puncture. D. Hepatitis A spreads faecal-orally and is not relevant to a contaminated puncture wound. E. A group and screen is for anticipated major blood loss, not a small puncture wound.
pearl: Every contaminated wound needs two questions answered: how tetanus-prone is it, and how many tetanus vaccine doses has the patient had?
thinking: Deep puncture wound with soil  ↓  Tetanus-prone wound  ↓  Older adult, immunisation may be incomplete  ↓  Check vaccine history to decide on booster and/or immunoglobulin
exam_trap: Option B is tempting for a 'deep' wound, but CK and renal function belong to crush and electrical injuries, not a contaminated puncture.
takeaway: For any contaminated wound, assess tetanus vaccination history and wound risk.
notes: Dropped at independent check: Duplicates live BX421 (contaminated puncture wound, key: wound nature and vaccination history determine tetanus management) in scenario and learning point; ID025 and UQ15832 also cover it. Distractors (thyroid, hepatitis A, group and screen) were also implausible.

stem:
A 9-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department 45 minutes after a neighbour's dog bit his forearm. There are several ragged puncture marks with saliva and bits of grass in them. The bleeding has stopped and he can move his fingers normally.

What is the most important initial step in managing the wound?

options.A: Close every puncture tightly with sutures straight away
options.B: Apply a topical steroid cream and a dry dressing
options.C: Explore, irrigate and clean the wound thoroughly
options.D: Splint the whole arm in a cast for two weeks
options.E: No treatment, because the bleeding has already stopped

correct_answer: C. Explore, irrigate and clean the wound thoroughly
why_correct: Dog bites inoculate oral bacteria deep into tissue, so the priority is thorough exploration and irrigation with plenty of warm running water or saline, removal of debris and assessment for damage to deep structures. Decisions about antibiotic prophylaxis, tetanus status and whether the wound should be left open follow. Source: NICE CKS Bites – human and animal; NICE NG184, 2020.
why_wrong: A. Puncture bite wounds are generally not closed primarily because closure traps bacteria and raises the infection risk. B. Topical steroids do not prevent infection and may impair healing. D. Routine casting is not needed; immobilisation is only for specific injuries. E. Bites carry an infection risk even after the bleeding has stopped.
pearl: In any mammalian bite, thorough irrigation and debridement are the most effective way to prevent infection.
thinking: Contaminated dog bite  ↓  High risk of wound infection  ↓  Explore, irrigate and debride  ↓  Then decide on antibiotics, tetanus and closure
exam_trap: Option A appeals because the wound looks untidy, but primary closure of contaminated puncture bites increases infection risk.
takeaway: Clean and irrigate every bite thoroughly before anything else.
notes: New vignette (child, UK domestic dog). Same learning point and key. Near BX186 is a rabies-endemic travel bite; different scenario and emphasis (rabies risk).

stem:
A 38-year-old electrician touched a high-voltage cable at work. He has a small charred mark on his right palm and a similar small mark on the sole of his left foot. He says he feels fine and wants to go back to work.

What is the most appropriate next step in his assessment?

options.A: Dress both burns and let him return to work this afternoon
options.B: Book a burns clinic review for later in the week
options.C: Request X-rays of the hand and foot only
options.D: ECG, creatine kinase and a search for deep tissue injury
options.E: Apply a topical antimicrobial cream and review in 48 hours

correct_answer: D. ECG, creatine kinase and a search for deep tissue injury
why_correct: Entry (palm) and exit (foot) wounds after a high-voltage contact mean current has passed through the body, so the small skin burns can hide extensive muscle, nerve and vessel damage, with a risk of rhabdomyolysis, acute kidney injury and compartment syndrome, and the current may have crossed the heart. He needs a 12-lead ECG with cardiac monitoring, creatine kinase, renal function and urine testing for myoglobin, and careful assessment for deep injury with referral to a burns service, even though he feels well. Source: Resuscitation Council UK Guidelines, 2025 (special circumstances); British Burn Association referral guidance.
why_wrong: A. Feeling well does not exclude deep tissue damage or arrhythmia, so returning to work without investigation is unsafe. B. A high-voltage electrical injury needs prompt assessment and burns-service referral, not a delayed clinic review. C. X-rays show neither muscle injury nor arrhythmia, and the danger lies along the current's path rather than in the bones of the hand and foot. E. Topical treatment deals only with the visible surface burn, which grossly underestimates the injury.
pearl: With electrical injury, the skin shows only where current entered and left; the damage lies along the path in between.
thinking: High-voltage contact  ↓  Small entry and exit burns  ↓  Current path through muscle and heart  ↓  ECG and monitoring, CK and renal function, look for deep injury
exam_trap: Option A appeals because he feels well and the burns look trivial, but the skin marks grossly underestimate the internal injury.
takeaway: Small electrical burns can hide major deep tissue damage and arrhythmia.
notes: New vignette (high-voltage workplace injury with entry and exit wounds). Same learning point and key. Near BX413 (factory shock, small burn, answer arrhythmia) is close; this version adds the entry/exit path and deep tissue injury angle, which matches the original key 'internal injury and arrhythmia'. Reviewer may wish to confirm it is distinct enough.

stem:
A 19-year-old university student is ready for discharge after hospital treatment for a severe allergic reaction to cashew nuts, with throat tightness and wheeze. She is being supplied with adrenaline auto-injectors before she leaves.

Which advice about the auto-injectors is most appropriate?

options.A: Use one straight away for anaphylaxis, then call 999
options.B: Take an antihistamine first and use a pen only if that fails
options.C: Keep one pen at home in a safe place, such as the fridge
options.D: Use a pen only once the ambulance crew have arrived
options.E: No hospital visit is needed if symptoms settle after a pen

correct_answer: A. Use one straight away for anaphylaxis, then call 999
why_correct: Adrenaline is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis and delay in giving it is associated with death, so she should use an auto-injector at the first signs of airway, breathing or circulation problems, then call 999 and say 'anaphylaxis'. MHRA advice is to carry two in-date auto-injectors at all times and know how to use them (a trainer device helps), using the second if there is no improvement after about five minutes. Source: MHRA Drug Safety Update, adrenaline auto-injectors, 2023; Resuscitation Council UK, 2021.
why_wrong: B. Antihistamines do not treat airway, breathing or circulatory compromise, and waiting for them delays adrenaline. C. Two in-date pens should be carried at all times, and they should not be refrigerated. D. Adrenaline should be given immediately, not delayed until help arrives. E. Emergency assessment is still needed after using a pen because symptoms can recur.
pearl: Two pens, always carried, used early, followed by a 999 call.
thinking: Previous anaphylaxis  ↓  Adrenaline auto-injectors prescribed  ↓  Teach recognition and immediate use  ↓  Call 999 after use; second pen if no improvement
exam_trap: Option B mirrors a common lay belief, but antihistamines are not first-line for anaphylaxis and waiting for them delays life-saving adrenaline.
takeaway: Anaphylaxis means adrenaline first, then 999.
notes: New vignette (student with nut anaphylaxis at discharge). Same learning point and key. Verified against MHRA advice (carry two in-date pens at all times).

stem:
A 55-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes arrives by ambulance with 50 minutes of heavy central chest discomfort, nausea and sweating. Her 12-lead ECG shows new ST elevation in leads I, aVL, V5 and V6. A high-sensitivity troponin taken on arrival is reported as within the normal range.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Repeat the troponin in three hours before deciding on treatment
options.B: Arrange an exercise ECG once her symptoms have settled
options.C: Activate the emergency reperfusion pathway immediately
options.D: Treat as reflux with a proton pump inhibitor and review
options.E: Refer her routinely to the cardiology outpatient clinic

correct_answer: C. Activate the emergency reperfusion pathway immediately
why_correct: Ischaemic chest pain with new ST elevation in contiguous leads is a STEMI, which is diagnosed clinically and on the ECG; troponin can still be normal soon after symptom onset. NICE advises immediate assessment for coronary reperfusion, usually primary PCI if it can be delivered in time and otherwise fibrinolysis, so a normal early troponin must not delay activation. Source: NICE NG185, Acute coronary syndromes, 2020.
why_wrong: A. Waiting for serial troponins delays reperfusion and belongs to the pathway for suspected NSTEMI, not STEMI. B. Exercise testing is contraindicated during an acute coronary syndrome. D. Ongoing ischaemic pain with ST elevation must not be attributed to reflux. E. A STEMI is an emergency and cannot wait for a routine referral.
pearl: STEMI is an ECG diagnosis: an early normal troponin never delays reperfusion.
thinking: Ischaemic chest pain  ↓  New ST elevation in contiguous lateral leads  ↓  Early troponin may be normal  ↓  Activate primary PCI/reperfusion pathway now
exam_trap: Option A tempts candidates who rely on biomarkers, but troponin rises take hours and serial testing is for suspected NSTEMI.
takeaway: In STEMI, act on the ECG, not the troponin.
notes: Re-angled: near ACU003, CARD001 and ACU028 already test 'STEMI -> primary PCI'. This version keeps the same key (activate reperfusion) but the scenario is a lateral STEMI in a woman with diabetes and an early normal troponin, so the learning point is the original's 'do not wait for troponin'. Distinct scenario from the near items.

stem:
A 63-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is brought in with a hot, swollen, foul-smelling foot ulcer. He is drowsy and breathing fast, with a low blood pressure and a rapid pulse. The admitting team suggests waiting for an MRI of the foot to confirm osteomyelitis before deciding on treatment.

Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Await the MRI result so that antibiotics can be targeted
options.B: Give paracetamol and repeat his observations in four hours
options.C: Wait for blood culture results before starting antibiotics
options.D: Treat as sepsis now and assess for organ dysfunction
options.E: Arrange a lumbar puncture to exclude meningitis first

correct_answer: D. Treat as sepsis now and assess for organ dysfunction
why_correct: Drowsiness, tachypnoea, hypotension and tachycardia with an infected diabetic foot place him at high risk of severe illness or death from sepsis. NICE NG253 requires immediate senior review, blood cultures, lactate and other bloods, and broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics within one hour with fluid resuscitation; imaging to define the source and plan surgery should follow rather than delay treatment. Source: NICE NG253, Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over, 2025 (updated 2026).
why_wrong: A. Source imaging is important but must not delay time-critical antibiotics and resuscitation. B. Treating the fever and deferring review ignores clear signs of shock. C. Cultures should be taken first, but antibiotics must not wait for the results. E. There are no features of meningitis, and a lumbar puncture would only delay treatment.
pearl: In high-risk sepsis, investigations to find the source run alongside treatment, never ahead of it.
thinking: Infected diabetic foot  ↓  Drowsy, tachypnoeic, hypotensive, tachycardic  ↓  High risk of severe illness from sepsis  ↓  Senior review, cultures, IV antibiotics and fluids now; image the source afterwards
exam_trap: Option A sounds like good antimicrobial stewardship, but in a shocked patient targeting can wait while delay cannot.
takeaway: Suspected sepsis with organ dysfunction is treated immediately; source imaging must not hold up antibiotics.
notes: New vignette (infected diabetic foot, team proposing MRI first) replacing the pneumonia stem. Same learning point and key. Similar principle to PAN211 in this batch but a different scenario and distractor set.

stem:
An 81-year-old woman with known left ventricular systolic dysfunction is woken at night by severe breathlessness. She is sitting bolt upright, coughing pink frothy sputum, and has fine crackles to both mid-zones. Her oxygen saturation is in the low 80s on room air and her blood pressure is well maintained.

What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Increase her oral furosemide and review her in clinic
options.B: Give a rapid intravenous fluid bolus for presumed sepsis
options.C: Lie her flat for a chest X-ray before starting treatment
options.D: Book an outpatient echocardiogram within two weeks
options.E: Sit her up, give oxygen and intravenous furosemide

correct_answer: E. Sit her up, give oxygen and intravenous furosemide
why_correct: Orthopnoea, pink frothy sputum, bilateral crackles and severe hypoxaemia in a patient with known LV dysfunction indicate acute pulmonary oedema, a medical emergency. She should be sat upright, given oxygen to correct hypoxaemia, and treated with intravenous loop diuretic, with escalation to non-invasive ventilation if she does not improve; NICE advises against routine opiates and nitrates. Source: NICE CG187, Acute heart failure, 2014 (updated 2021).
why_wrong: A. Severe hypoxaemia with pulmonary oedema needs hospital treatment with intravenous diuretic, not an oral dose change and clinic review. B. A fluid bolus would worsen pulmonary oedema. C. Lying flat worsens breathlessness, and treatment should not wait for imaging. D. An outpatient echo does nothing for an acute emergency.
