pearl: Acute pulmonary oedema: sit up, oxygen, IV loop diuretic, and consider CPAP early if she does not respond.
thinking: Known LV dysfunction  ↓  Night-time orthopnoea, frothy sputum, bilateral crackles  ↓  Severe hypoxaemia  ↓  Acute pulmonary oedema: upright, oxygen, IV furosemide, escalate if needed
exam_trap: Option C looks like sensible diagnostic sequencing, but lying a patient with pulmonary oedema flat can precipitate respiratory arrest.
takeaway: Acute pulmonary oedema is an emergency: oxygen and intravenous diuretic without delay.
notes: New vignette (older woman, nocturnal pulmonary oedema). Key made more specific (oxygen and IV furosemide) but is the same management as the original 'oxygen and acute heart-failure therapy'. Verified against NICE CG187 (IV diuretic; no routine opiates or nitrates). Exact saturation figure softened to 'low 80s'.

stem:
A 58-year-old woman who flew back from Australia a week ago, and has had a swollen left calf since, collapses in the emergency department waiting room. She is breathless, cyanosed and cold to the touch, with a very low blood pressure and a raised jugular venous pressure. A bedside echocardiogram shows a dilated, poorly contracting right ventricle.

What is the most appropriate immediate approach?

options.A: Start a DOAC and book a CT pulmonary angiogram for tomorrow
options.B: High-risk PE: urgent senior input and consider thrombolysis
options.C: Check a D-dimer and anticoagulate only if it is raised
options.D: Wait for troponin and BNP to risk-stratify before treating
options.E: Arrange a ventilation-perfusion scan on the next routine list

correct_answer: B. High-risk PE: urgent senior input and consider thrombolysis
why_correct: Collapse with shock, a raised JVP and an acutely dilated right ventricle after long-haul travel with a swollen calf indicates haemodynamically unstable (high-risk) pulmonary embolism. She needs immediate resuscitation and senior and critical care input; NICE advises continuous unfractionated heparin and considering systemic thrombolysis, and bedside echo evidence of right ventricular dysfunction can support treatment when she is too unstable for CT. Source: NICE NG158, Venous thromboembolic diseases, 2020; ESC acute PE guideline, 2019.
why_wrong: A. Oral anticoagulation with next-day imaging is the pathway for haemodynamically stable patients. C. D-dimer testing has no role in a shocked patient with a high clinical probability of PE. D. Biomarkers give prognostic information but must not delay treatment of shock. E. A routine V/Q scan is far too slow and unsafe in an unstable patient.
pearl: Shock plus suspected PE changes everything: think thrombolysis, not routine diagnostic sequencing.
thinking: Recent long-haul flight and swollen calf  ↓  Collapse with shock and raised JVP  ↓  Dilated right ventricle on bedside echo  ↓  High-risk PE: resuscitate, UFH, senior input, consider thrombolysis
exam_trap: Option A is the correct pathway for a stable patient, which is exactly why it tempts; instability makes it unsafe here.
takeaway: Suspected PE with haemodynamic instability is an emergency for senior-led thrombolysis decisions.
notes: Dropped at independent check: Duplicate. Same scenario and learning point as PAN1412 in this batch (long-haul flight, swollen calf, collapse with shock, key: treat as high-risk PE with urgent senior input) and same learning point as PAN1271 (postoperative shocked PE, same key); CARD028 already covers thrombolysis. Clinically accurate, but a third copy of the same point adds nothing. If C1 retires both PAN1271 and PAN1412, reinstate PAN207 instead.

stem:
A 47-year-old woman attends the emergency department with three days of dysuria, rigors and right loin pain. Over the past hour she has become disorientated; she is cold and clammy, her blood pressure is low and she is getting worse.

What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Arrange a CT scan to find the source before starting fluids
options.B: Take blood cultures and start antibiotics once they are positive
options.C: Start the sepsis pathway: cultures, then immediate treatment
options.D: Give oral antibiotics and arrange GP follow-up within 48 hours
options.E: Book an outpatient renal ultrasound and clinic review

correct_answer: C. Start the sepsis pathway: cultures, then immediate treatment
why_correct: She has suspected urosepsis with high-risk features: new confusion, hypotension and deterioration. NICE NG253 advises immediate senior review, blood cultures and bloods including lactate, then broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics within one hour and intravenous fluid resuscitation; imaging to look for an obstructed kidney follows urgently but must not delay treatment. Source: NICE NG253, Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over, 2024 (amended 2025).
why_wrong: A. Resuscitation and antibiotics must not wait for imaging. B. Waiting for positive cultures would delay antibiotics by a day or more. D. Oral treatment at home is unsafe for a hypotensive, deteriorating patient. E. Routine outpatient tests ignore a life-threatening emergency.
pearl: Take cultures first, but never let cultures or scans delay the first antibiotic dose in high-risk sepsis.
thinking: Pyelonephritis symptoms  ↓  New confusion, hypotension, worsening  ↓  High risk of severe illness from sepsis  ↓  Cultures, then IV antibiotics and fluids within the hour; image the kidney urgently
exam_trap: Option B contains a correct step (blood cultures) bolted to an unsafe one (waiting for the result).
takeaway: In high-risk sepsis, cultures come first and antibiotics follow immediately, not after the results.
notes: Dropped at independent check: Duplicate. Scenario and learning point match live RES007 (woman with UTI, acutely confused, hypotensive -> start sepsis bundle immediately); the 'image first' and 'wait for cultures' distractors are already taught by PAN243 and PAN205 in this batch. Also cites NG253 as '2024 (amended 2025)'; NG253 was published 19 Nov 2025, last updated 23 Sep 2026.

stem:
A 27-year-old woman whose mother and aunt have had recurrent 'swelling attacks' develops a rapidly enlarging tongue and swollen lips a few hours after a dental extraction. There is no itch or rash. Her voice has become muffled.

Which life-threatening complication must be assessed for first?

options.A: Acute kidney injury from dehydration
options.B: Perforation of the small bowel
options.C: Prolonged generalised seizures
options.D: Upper airway obstruction
options.E: Acute retention of urine

correct_answer: D. Upper airway obstruction
why_correct: Recurrent non-itchy swellings with a family history, triggered by dental trauma, suggest hereditary angioedema, and tongue swelling with a change in voice means the upper airway is involved. Airway obstruction can develop rapidly and is the main cause of death, so the airway must be assessed immediately with early anaesthetic and ENT involvement; specific treatment is C1-esterase inhibitor concentrate or icatibant, because adrenaline and antihistamines are often ineffective. Source: NICE CKS Angio-oedema and anaphylaxis, 2024.
why_wrong: A. Kidney injury is not the immediate threat from orofacial swelling. B. Abdominal attacks of angioedema cause pain and vomiting, but perforation is not the main danger here. C. Seizures are not a feature of angioedema. E. Urinary retention is unrelated to tongue and lip swelling.
pearl: Whatever the cause of angioedema, tongue swelling or voice change means the airway comes first.
thinking: Family history of swelling attacks  ↓  Non-itchy lip and tongue swelling after dental work  ↓  Muffled voice  ↓  Upper airway at risk: assess and protect the airway now
exam_trap: Option B tempts candidates who know hereditary angioedema can affect the gut, but abdominal attacks are painful rather than the immediate life threat.
takeaway: Lip and tongue swelling threatens the airway: assess it before anything else.
notes: New vignette (hereditary angioedema triggered by dental extraction) so it does not duplicate BX035 (peanut allergy teenager, same answer 'airway compromise'). Same learning point and key. Distractors reworded to the same type.

stem:
A 66-year-old woman is recovering on a surgical ward after a bowel resection. A CT pulmonary angiogram this morning confirmed a pulmonary embolism. This afternoon she becomes grey and clammy, her blood pressure drops sharply and stays low despite a fluid bolus, and her neck veins are distended.

How should her pulmonary embolism now be classified?

options.A: Low-risk PE suitable for outpatient treatment
options.B: Intermediate-risk PE with right heart strain only
options.C: Pulmonary infarction causing pleuritic pain alone
options.D: A vasovagal reaction to her heparin injection
options.E: High-risk PE with haemodynamic instability

correct_answer: E. High-risk PE with haemodynamic instability
why_correct: Sustained hypotension with signs of shock and raised venous pressure in a patient with PE indicates obstructive shock from right ventricular failure, which defines high-risk ('massive'), haemodynamically unstable PE. This changes management: NICE NG158 advises continuous unfractionated heparin and considering thrombolysis, with urgent senior input, although her recent surgery makes bleeding risk a key part of that decision. Source: NICE NG158, Venous thromboembolic diseases, 2020.
why_wrong: A. Outpatient care is only for haemodynamically stable, low-risk PE. B. Intermediate-risk PE involves right ventricular strain without hypotension or shock. C. Pulmonary infarction causes pleuritic pain and haemoptysis but not shock with distended neck veins. D. A vasovagal episode is brief and self-limiting with low neck veins, not sustained hypotension with a raised JVP.
pearl: It is haemodynamic status, not clot size on the scan, that makes a pulmonary embolism high risk.
thinking: Confirmed PE  ↓  Sustained hypotension despite fluid  ↓  Raised JVP: right ventricular failure  ↓  High-risk (unstable) PE: senior review, UFH, consider thrombolysis
exam_trap: Option B tempts because right heart strain is present, but once hypotension and shock develop the PE is high-risk, not intermediate.
takeaway: PE with shock or sustained hypotension is high-risk PE and a medical emergency.
notes: Dropped at independent check: Duplicate. The learning point (PE with shock/sustained hypotension = high-risk, haemodynamically unstable PE) is already live in BX265 (and UQ12825), and the scenario (postoperative patient with PE who becomes shocked, fluid-unresponsive, raised JVP) is effectively PAN1271 in this batch. Adds nothing distinct.

stem:
A 74-year-old man who had a coronary stent inserted last year and takes aspirin and clopidogrel is found by his wife on the bathroom floor after vomiting a large amount of dark 'coffee-ground' material. He has also passed black, tarry stool. In the emergency department he is pale, sweaty and muddled, with a fast pulse and a low blood pressure.

What should be done first?

options.A: ABCDE assessment and resuscitation with IV access
options.B: Oral PPI and an outpatient endoscopy next week
options.C: Urgent colonoscopy to find the bleeding point
options.D: Oral iron and a repeat full blood count in a month
options.E: Discharge him if the vomiting settles in the department

correct_answer: A. ABCDE assessment and resuscitation with IV access
why_correct: Haematemesis and melaena with a fast pulse, low blood pressure and confusion indicate a major upper GI bleed with shock, most likely from a peptic ulcer in a man on dual antiplatelet therapy. The first priority is ABCDE assessment and resuscitation (large-bore IV access, bloods including cross-match, fluids and blood as needed, senior help), and NICE advises endoscopy immediately after resuscitation in unstable patients. Whether to continue clopidogrel is decided afterwards with a cardiologist, because stopping it after a recent stent carries its own risk. Source: NICE CG141, Acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding in over 16s, 2012 (updated 2016).
why_wrong: B. NICE advises against PPIs before endoscopy in suspected non-variceal bleeding, and outpatient endoscopy is unsafe in a shocked patient. C. Colonoscopy does not examine the upper GI tract, and any investigation must follow resuscitation. D. Iron does not address active haemorrhage. E. A pause in vomiting does not mean the bleeding has stopped or that he is safe.
pearl: In upper GI bleeding with shock, resuscitate first, then scope immediately afterwards.
thinking: Aspirin and clopidogrel after a coronary stent  ↓  Haematemesis and melaena  ↓  Fast pulse, low blood pressure, confusion  ↓  ABCDE and resuscitation, then urgent endoscopy
exam_trap: Option B combines two errors: PPI before endoscopy is not recommended by NICE, and outpatient endoscopy ignores her shock.
takeaway: Unstable upper GI bleed: resuscitate before any investigation.
notes: Checker C2: re-angled from an NSAID user (duplicated UAKT029) to dual antiplatelet therapy after a coronary stent. Same learning point and key. CG141 recs 1.3.1, 1.4.3 and 1.6.3 (clopidogrel decision with cardiologist).

stem:
A 64-year-old woman who was treated for breast cancer three years ago has had worsening mid-back pain for a fortnight, now with a tight, band-like pain around her chest that is worse when she coughs. Today she says her legs feel heavy and she has stumbled twice.

Which diagnosis must be urgently considered?

options.A: Mechanical thoracic back pain
options.B: Metastatic spinal cord compression
options.C: Peripheral neuropathy from chemotherapy
options.D: Osteoporotic vertebral fracture
options.E: Fibromyalgia with widespread pain

correct_answer: B. Metastatic spinal cord compression
why_correct: Progressive thoracic back pain with band-like radicular pain and new leg heaviness in someone with a history of cancer is metastatic spinal cord compression until proven otherwise; breast cancer commonly spreads to the spine. NICE advises immediate contact with the MSCC coordinator, an urgent whole-spine MRI, and dexamethasone as soon as possible for neurological symptoms or signs. Source: NICE NG234, Spinal metastases and metastatic spinal cord compression, 2023.
why_wrong: A. Mechanical pain does not cause band-like radicular pain with progressive leg weakness, and her cancer history is a red flag. C. Chemotherapy neuropathy causes symmetrical distal sensory symptoms, not back pain with progressive weakness. D. A fracture alone does not explain the evolving neurology, and in a cancer survivor a collapsed vertebra must be presumed pathological until proven otherwise. E. Fibromyalgia does not cause objective, progressive weakness.
pearl: Back pain plus a cancer history plus any new neurology means MSCC until an MRI says otherwise.
thinking: Previous breast cancer  ↓  Progressive thoracic pain, band-like and worse on coughing  ↓  New leg heaviness and falls  ↓  Suspect MSCC: urgent MRI whole spine and dexamethasone
exam_trap: Option D tempts in an older woman with back pain, but new neurological symptoms after cancer demand exclusion of cord compression.
takeaway: New neurology with back pain in a patient with a cancer history is MSCC until proven otherwise.
notes: New vignette (breast cancer survivor, thoracic radicular pain) so it does not repeat NEU121 (prostate cancer, same recognition with management answer). Same learning point and key. MRI timing figure omitted.

stem:
A 52-year-old man with non-Hodgkin lymphoma had his second cycle of chemotherapy eight days ago. His partner brings him to the emergency department after finding him shivering and hot; his temperature is raised, but his blood pressure is normal and he says he feels only 'a bit washed out'. His neutrophil count is very low.

What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Await blood culture results before choosing antibiotics
options.B: Paracetamol and a routine oncology clinic review
options.C: Reassure him that fevers are common after chemotherapy
options.D: Treat as an emergency with immediate IV antibiotics
options.E: Start oral iron and recheck the blood count next week

correct_answer: D. Treat as an emergency with immediate IV antibiotics
why_correct: Fever in a patient with chemotherapy-induced neutropenia is suspected neutropenic sepsis, which can progress rapidly to septic shock even when the patient looks well. NICE advises treating it as an acute medical emergency: take cultures and bloods, then give empirical intravenous antibiotics (piperacillin with tazobactam unless contraindicated) immediately, without waiting for results. Source: NICE CG151, Neutropenic sepsis, 2012.
why_wrong: A. Cultures should be taken first, but antibiotics must not be delayed for results. B. Antipyretics and delayed review mask the fever and delay treatment of a potentially fatal infection. C. Fever in a neutropenic patient must be assumed to be infection until proven otherwise. E. Iron has no role; the problem is neutropenia, not anaemia.
pearl: A neutropenic patient may look deceptively well before collapsing; the fever alone is the alarm.
thinking: Recent chemotherapy  ↓  Fever with very low neutrophils  ↓  Suspected neutropenic sepsis  ↓  Cultures, then immediate IV piperacillin with tazobactam
exam_trap: Option C tempts because he looks well, but neutropenic patients cannot mount normal signs of infection and can deteriorate quickly.
takeaway: Fever after chemotherapy with neutropenia is an emergency for immediate IV antibiotics.
notes: Dropped at independent check: Duplicate. Same scenario and learning point as live HAE028 and HAE041 (fever on chemotherapy, neutropenia, haemodynamically stable -> immediate IV broad-spectrum antibiotics such as piperacillin/tazobactam) and ACU049. PAN2433 in this batch already covers the replaced point from a distinct angle (telephone triage).

stem:
A 33-year-old man who smokes develops sudden left-sided chest pain and breathlessness while sitting at his desk. Within minutes he is grey and sweaty, with a falling blood pressure, a trachea pushed to the right and a silent, hyper-resonant left hemithorax. His oxygen saturation keeps dropping despite high-flow oxygen.

What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Portable chest X-ray first to confirm the diagnosis
options.B: CT chest to look for underlying bullous lung disease
options.C: IV antibiotics for presumed left lower lobe pneumonia
options.D: Oxygen alone with reassessment in an hour
options.E: Immediate decompression without waiting for imaging

correct_answer: E. Immediate decompression without waiting for imaging
why_correct: Hypotension, worsening hypoxaemia, tracheal deviation and a silent hyper-resonant hemithorax after a sudden pneumothorax indicate tension physiology, which can cause cardiac arrest within minutes. It is a clinical diagnosis and needs immediate decompression followed by chest drain insertion, rather than delay for imaging. Source: BTS Guideline for pleural disease, 2023.
why_wrong: A. Waiting for an X-ray delays life-saving treatment when tension pneumothorax is clinically evident. B. CT has a role later in recurrent or complicated pneumothorax, not in an unstable patient. C. The sudden onset with tracheal deviation and hyper-resonance points to pneumothorax, not pneumonia. D. Oxygen alone does not relieve rising intrapleural pressure, and he is deteriorating.
pearl: Tension pneumothorax is diagnosed at the bedside and treated before any X-ray.
thinking: Sudden pleuritic pain and breathlessness  ↓  Hypotension, tracheal deviation, silent hyper-resonant side  ↓  Tension physiology  ↓  Immediate decompression, then chest drain
exam_trap: Option A feels like good practice, but an X-ray in a peri-arrest tension pneumothorax costs minutes the patient does not have.
takeaway: Suspected tension pneumothorax with haemodynamic compromise needs decompression now, not imaging.
notes: New vignette (spontaneous, non-traumatic tension in a smoker at work); key made explicit (immediate decompression) but same management as the original 'treat immediately as tension pneumothorax'. Near ACU030/RES009 test decompression before imaging in TRAUMA; RES017 is a stable spontaneous pneumothorax; 240 tests the diagnosis. Different scenario, so not treated as a duplicate.

stem:
A 41-year-old woman phones her GP practice. For two weeks she and her teenage son have woken with throbbing headaches and nausea that ease once they are out at work and school. Their cat has become lethargic, and she has noticed that the flame on her old gas fire burns orange rather than blue.

What should she be advised to do immediately?

options.A: Leave the house now and seek urgent medical assessment
options.B: Take paracetamol and keep a headache diary for a month
options.C: Keep the fire on with a window open until it is serviced
options.D: Book a routine appointment to discuss migraine prevention
options.E: Start a course of antibiotics for presumed sinusitis

correct_answer: A. Leave the house now and seek urgent medical assessment
why_correct: Headaches and nausea affecting several members of a household (and a pet) that improve away from home, with a gas appliance burning with an orange flame, strongly suggest carbon monoxide poisoning. The priority is to stop exposure: switch off the appliance if it is safe to do so, get out into fresh air, call the National Gas Helpline, and seek urgent medical assessment, where high-flow oxygen is given. Source: NHS, Carbon monoxide poisoning, 2025.
why_wrong: B. Analgesia and watchful waiting allow continued, potentially fatal exposure. C. An open window does not make a faulty appliance safe. D. Labelling this as migraine misses an environmental poisoning affecting the whole household. E. Antibiotics have no role, and sinusitis would not explain symptoms in several people that ease away from home.
pearl: Symptoms shared by people (and pets) in one building that improve on leaving it are carbon monoxide until proven otherwise.
thinking: Headache and nausea in several household members  ↓  Better away from home; sick pet  ↓  Orange gas flame  ↓  Suspected CO: remove from source, gas helpline, urgent medical assessment
exam_trap: Option D tempts because recurrent headaches suggest migraine, but the household pattern and appliance clue point to an environmental cause.
takeaway: Suspected carbon monoxide exposure: get out of the building and get assessed urgently.
notes: New vignette (telephone call to GP, family and pet affected, orange flame). Same learning point and key. Near CP032 tests hospital treatment (100% oxygen), not the immediate advice. Advice checked against NHS CO page (reviewed Dec 2025) and National Gas Helpline guidance.

stem:
During a week-long summer heatwave, a carer finds an 83-year-old woman who lives alone in a top-floor flat drowsy and muddled. Her skin is hot and dry, and her core temperature is markedly raised. She has had no vomiting or diarrhoea and has started no new medicines.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Heat exhaustion
options.B: Heat stroke
options.C: Viral gastroenteritis
options.D: Hypothermia
options.E: Panic attack

correct_answer: B. Heat stroke
why_correct: Core hyperthermia with an altered mental state during a heatwave is classic (non-exertional) heat stroke, to which older people living alone in hot, poorly ventilated homes are especially vulnerable. Central nervous system dysfunction is what separates it from heat exhaustion, and it is a medical emergency needing rapid active cooling and supportive care. Source: NHS, Heat exhaustion and heatstroke, 2026; UKHSA heat-health guidance.
why_wrong: A. Heat exhaustion causes weakness, sweating and nausea, but the mental state remains normal. C. Gastroenteritis would cause vomiting or diarrhoea, which she has not had. D. Hypothermia is a low, not a raised, core temperature. E. A panic attack does not cause a markedly raised core temperature with drowsiness.
pearl: Confusion is the dividing line: heat illness with altered mental state is heat stroke, not heat exhaustion.
thinking: Older woman alone during a heatwave  ↓  Markedly raised core temperature  ↓  Drowsy and confused  ↓  CNS dysfunction = heat stroke; cool rapidly
exam_trap: Option A is the closest distractor, but heat exhaustion does not cause confusion or drowsiness.
takeaway: Hyperthermia with confusion in a heatwave is heat stroke, a medical emergency.
notes: New vignette (classic, non-exertional heat stroke in an isolated older woman). Added heat exhaustion as the key discriminating distractor (mental state, not a temperature cut-off). Near BX698 is exertional heat stroke in a young worker with a stated temperature; different scenario.

stem:
A 6-year-old girl is pulled from the deep end of a public pool by a lifeguard after being under water briefly. She is now conscious and crying but keeps coughing, is breathing fast and has crackles at both lung bases.

What is the immediate priority?

options.A: Induce vomiting to clear any swallowed water
options.B: Give oral fluids to replace losses and calm her
options.C: Support airway and breathing, with oxygen
options.D: Start prophylactic antibiotics against aspiration
options.E: Let her go home once she has stopped crying

correct_answer: C. Support airway and breathing, with oxygen
why_correct: Drowning injures the lungs through aspiration and hypoxia, so a child who is coughing, tachypnoeic and has crackles after submersion has respiratory compromise. The priority is assessment and support of airway and breathing with high-flow oxygen and monitoring, followed by hospital observation because lung injury can worsen over the following hours. Source: Resuscitation Council UK, Special circumstances guidelines (drowning), 2021.
why_wrong: A. Inducing vomiting is never indicated and increases the risk of aspirating gastric contents. B. Oral fluids risk aspiration and do nothing for hypoxia. D. Prophylactic antibiotics are not routinely recommended and do not address the immediate threat. E. Respiratory symptoms after submersion need hospital assessment and observation, as deterioration may be delayed.
pearl: The core problem in drowning is hypoxia, so airway, breathing and oxygen always come first.
thinking: Submersion in a pool  ↓  Cough, tachypnoea, crackles  ↓  Aspiration and hypoxia  ↓  Support airway and breathing with oxygen, then observe in hospital
exam_trap: Option E tempts because she is conscious and crying, but respiratory signs after submersion can progress over hours.
takeaway: After drowning, assess and support airway and breathing first.
notes: New vignette (conscious child with chest signs) so it differs from BX414 (unconscious adult man, same principle). Same learning point and key.

stem:
A 36-year-old woman got a jolt from a frayed hairdryer flex at home and felt tingling up her arm. There is no visible burn. An hour later she comes to the emergency department because her heart feels as though it is 'racing and missing beats'.

Which complication should be specifically assessed?

options.A: Cataract formation
options.B: Acute appendicitis
options.C: Middle-ear infection
options.D: Peptic ulceration
options.E: Cardiac arrhythmia

correct_answer: E. Cardiac arrhythmia
why_correct: Electric current crossing the chest can disturb cardiac conduction, and palpitations after a shock suggest an arrhythmia. She needs a 12-lead ECG and a period of cardiac monitoring, whereas an asymptomatic patient with a normal ECG after a low-voltage domestic shock usually needs no prolonged monitoring. Source: Resuscitation Council UK, Special circumstances (electrocution), 2021.
why_wrong: A. Cataract is a late complication, mainly of high-voltage injury, and does not explain palpitations. B. Appendicitis is unrelated to an electric shock. C. Middle-ear infection is an infective condition unrelated to electrical injury. D. Peptic ulceration is not an acute complication of electric shock and does not cause palpitations.
pearl: After any electric shock, palpitations, chest pain or an abnormal ECG mean monitoring.
thinking: Domestic electric shock  ↓  No visible burn  ↓  New palpitations  ↓  Possible arrhythmia: 12-lead ECG and cardiac monitoring
exam_trap: Option A is a genuine complication of electrical injury, but it develops late and does not explain her palpitations.
takeaway: Palpitations after an electric shock: look for an arrhythmia with an ECG and monitoring.
notes: New vignette (low-voltage domestic hairdryer shock, no burn). Same learning point and key. Distinct from PAN1937 in this batch (high-voltage, deep tissue) and from near BX413 (factory worker with burn mark, asymptomatic).

stem:
A 45-year-old builder is mixing wet cement when some splashes into his left eye. He arrives at the emergency department ten minutes later with a painful, watering, red eye and is struggling to keep it open.

What should be done first?

options.A: Cover the eye with a pad and refer to eye casualty
options.B: Irrigate the eye immediately and copiously
options.C: Await an ophthalmology review before treatment
options.D: Start steroid eye drops to reduce inflammation
options.E: Ask him to rub the eye to remove the particles

correct_answer: B. Irrigate the eye immediately and copiously
why_correct: Wet cement contains lime and is strongly alkaline; alkalis penetrate the eye quickly and cause severe, progressive damage. The immediate priority is copious irrigation with saline or water (after topical anaesthetic), sweeping the fornices to remove particles and continuing until the pH is neutral, with urgent ophthalmology assessment afterwards. Source: NHS, Eye injuries, 2026; Royal College of Ophthalmologists.
why_wrong: A. Padding before irrigation leaves the alkali in contact with the eye. C. Delay allows continued penetration, so irrigation must start before specialist review. D. Steroid drops are a later specialist decision and do not remove the chemical. E. Rubbing spreads the chemical and abrades the cornea.
pearl: In any chemical eye injury, irrigation starts before history, examination or referral, and continues until the pH is normal.
thinking: Cement splash to the eye  ↓  Alkali injury, rapidly penetrating  ↓  Irrigate immediately and copiously  ↓  Check pH, remove particles, then urgent ophthalmology review
exam_trap: Option A sounds like appropriate referral, but patching before irrigation traps the chemical against the cornea.
takeaway: Chemical eye injury: irrigate first, refer second.
notes: New vignette (alkali cement splash in a builder). Same learning point and key. Verified against NHS eye injuries page (reviewed Mar 2026: keep rinsing with water).

stem:
A 30-year-old chef catches the back of her hand in a brief burst of steam from a commercial dishwasher. When seen an hour later the area is uniformly red, dry and painful, with no blisters, and the redness fades briefly when pressed.

Which burn depth best fits these findings?

options.A: Full-thickness burn
options.B: Deep partial-thickness burn
options.C: Superficial (epidermal) burn
options.D: Superficial partial-thickness burn
options.E: Deep burn involving muscle

correct_answer: C. Superficial (epidermal) burn
why_correct: A burn confined to the epidermis is red, dry, painful and blanches on pressure without blisters, and it usually heals within about a week without scarring. Blistering would suggest superficial partial-thickness (dermal) involvement, while pale, blotchy or insensate areas suggest deeper injury. Source: NICE CKS, Burns and scalds, 2024.
why_wrong: A. Full-thickness burns are white, leathery or charred, painless and do not blanch. B. Deep partial-thickness burns look blotchy red or white, have reduced sensation and blanch poorly or not at all. D. Superficial partial-thickness burns are also painful and blanching, but they characteristically blister. E. Burns reaching muscle are insensate and charred and do not blanch.
pearl: Red, painful, blanching and no blisters means epidermal; add blisters and it is superficial partial-thickness.
thinking: Brief steam scald  ↓  Red, dry, painful, blanches  ↓  No blisters  ↓  Epidermal (superficial) burn
exam_trap: Option D is the closest distractor; the absence of blisters is what distinguishes an epidermal burn.
takeaway: A red, painful, blanching burn without blisters is a superficial epidermal burn.
notes: New vignette (steam scald in a chef). Added 'no blisters' to the stem and a superficial partial-thickness distractor so only one option fits; the original's 'painful, red, blanching' alone does not exclude superficial partial-thickness. Same learning point and key; implausible distractors (chemical, electrical) replaced with burn-depth categories of the same type.

stem:
A 66-year-old woman with a known stone in her left submandibular duct comes to the emergency department after two days of worsening pain under her jaw. The swelling has now spread across the front of her neck to both sides under the chin, the floor of her mouth is firm and her tongue is pushed upwards. She is sitting forward, drooling, and her speech sounds thick and muffled. Her temperature is 38.6°C.

What is the most immediate threat to her life?

options.A: Facial nerve palsy from gland inflammation
options.B: Dehydration from poor oral intake
options.C: Permanent loss of salivary gland function
options.D: Obstruction of the upper airway
options.E: Spread of infection to the parotid gland

correct_answer: D. Obstruction of the upper airway
why_correct: Firm bilateral swelling of the submandibular spaces and floor of the mouth, with the tongue lifted, drooling and a muffled voice, is Ludwig's angina; here it has spread from an infected salivary gland rather than a tooth. The swelling pushes the tongue up and back and can close the upper airway within hours, so keep her sitting up, call senior anaesthetic and ENT or maxillofacial help early, and start IV antibiotics; do not send her to lie flat for imaging before the airway has been assessed. Source: NICE CKS, Dental abscess (immediate admission for floor-of-mouth swelling or airway compromise), 2024.
why_wrong: A. The facial nerve runs through the parotid, not the submandibular gland, and a palsy would not threaten life. B. Poor intake matters, but it is easily corrected and is not the immediate danger. C. Loss of gland function is a late, minor consequence compared with airway obstruction. E. Spread to the parotid is not the expected direction of spread here, and the airway threat comes first.
pearl: Drooling, inability to swallow saliva, a muffled voice or a tongue pushed upwards in neck-space infection are warning signs that the airway is narrowing.
thinking: Infected submandibular gland  ↓  bilateral firm swelling of the floor of the mouth  ↓  tongue displaced upwards, drooling, muffled voice  ↓  Ludwig's angina  ↓  upper airway obstruction
exam_trap: B, dehydration — she cannot swallow and will need fluids, but this is a secondary problem; the airway can close long before dehydration matters.
takeaway: Floor-of-mouth swelling with drooling and a muffled voice is an airway emergency whatever the source of infection.
notes: Re-angled to a salivary-stone source (submandibular sialadenitis spreading to the floor of the mouth) because the dental-infection scenario duplicates BX236 (airway priority) and BX778 (Ludwig's diagnosis). Same learning point and key (airway compromise). NICE CKS page could not be fetched by curl (JS-only); source carried over from general CKS dental abscess admission criteria.

stem:
A 52-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with a day of fever, rigors and right upper abdominal pain, and his eyes have turned yellow. He is drowsy, his respiratory rate is 26 breaths per minute, heart rate 126 beats per minute, blood pressure 90/56 mmHg and his NEWS2 total is 9.

Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Repeat the observations in 1 hour, then decide on treatment
options.B: Send blood cultures and wait for growth before antibiotics
options.C: Request an ultrasound scan and review the patient afterwards
options.D: Give oral antibiotics and arrange a surgical clinic review
options.E: Urgent clinical review with IV antibiotics within the hour

correct_answer: E. Urgent clinical review with IV antibiotics within the hour
why_correct: With a likely infection (probable cholangitis) and a NEWS2 of 7 or more, NICE classes him as high risk of severe illness or death from sepsis. He needs urgent assessment by a clinician with acute-care competencies (FY2 or above), blood tests including cultures and lactate, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour, an IV fluid bolus, and referral to the senior clinical decision maker. Source: NICE NG253, Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over, 2025 (updated 2026).
why_wrong: A. Waiting an hour to re-score delays time-critical treatment in a high-risk patient. B. Cultures should be taken first, but antibiotics must not wait for culture results. C. Imaging is needed to find the source, but it should follow, not delay, resuscitation and antibiotics. D. Oral antibiotics and outpatient review are unsafe for someone who is hypotensive and drowsy.
pearl: In adults with suspected infection, a NEWS2 of 7 or more means high risk: think urgent review, antibiotics within the hour and senior involvement.
thinking: Fever, rigors, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain  ↓  likely biliary infection  ↓  drowsy, hypotensive, NEWS2 9  ↓  high risk of severe illness from sepsis  ↓  urgent review and IV antibiotics within 1 hour
exam_trap: C, ultrasound first — finding the source matters, but scanning before treatment wastes the first critical hour.
takeaway: Suspected sepsis with a NEWS2 of 7 or more needs urgent review and IV antibiotics within an hour.
notes: New ED scenario (probable cholangitis) instead of a generic inpatient. NEWS2 figure kept: PLAB relies on it and the score of 9 is well clear of the cut-off, so the key does not hinge on borderline recall. Checked against NG253 recs 1.6.2, 1.8.2–1.8.4 (Sept 2026 update). Distinct from GF040/ACU007/RES007 (escalation questions).

stem:
A 47-year-old woman phones the acute oncology helpline in the evening. She had her third cycle of chemotherapy for breast cancer 8 days ago and has just measured her temperature at 38.3°C. She feels shivery but says she is otherwise fine, and asks whether she can take paracetamol and see how she is in the morning.

What is the most appropriate interpretation of her symptoms?

options.A: Possible neutropenic sepsis needing hospital assessment now
options.B: A minor viral illness that can be managed with paracetamol
options.C: An expected reaction to chemotherapy that will settle alone
options.D: A delayed allergic reaction to a chemotherapy drug
options.E: Probable anaemia from chemotherapy needing a routine blood test

correct_answer: A. Possible neutropenic sepsis needing hospital assessment now
why_correct: Fever in the week or two after chemotherapy must be treated as neutropenic sepsis until proved otherwise, even if the person feels fairly well, because infection can progress very quickly when the neutrophil count is low. She should attend hospital immediately for assessment, blood tests and empirical IV antibiotics given without waiting for the neutrophil count. Source: NICE CG151, Neutropenic sepsis, 2012.
why_wrong: B. Assuming a viral illness and treating at home risks a rapid deterioration from bacterial sepsis, and paracetamol can mask the fever. C. Fever is not an expected effect of chemotherapy and must be presumed to be infection. D. A drug allergy does not explain fever 8 days after treatment and should not delay assessment for sepsis. E. Anaemia does not cause fever, and a routine test would dangerously delay treatment.
pearl: Feeling well does not exclude neutropenic sepsis; any fever in the days after chemotherapy needs same-hour assessment and antibiotics.
thinking: Chemotherapy 8 days ago  ↓  expected neutrophil nadir  ↓  new fever and shivering  ↓  cannot contain infection normally  ↓  possible neutropenic sepsis: attend hospital now
exam_trap: B, viral illness managed with paracetamol — it sounds proportionate for someone who feels fine, but it delays antibiotics and masks the fever.
takeaway: Fever after chemotherapy is neutropenic sepsis until proved otherwise: assess and treat immediately.
notes: Re-angled to telephone triage at home because the in-hospital scenarios (known low neutrophils, or count pending) already exist (BX579, HAE028, HAE041, ACU049, DR022). Same learning point and key meaning (neutropenic sepsis needing urgent treatment).

stem:
A 41-year-old woman is admitted from the emergency department with fever, loin pain and rigors and is being treated for sepsis from pyelonephritis. She has no lung disease, has never smoked and has no neuromuscular or chest wall problem. On air her pulse oximeter reads 89%.

Which oxygen saturation range should her prescription target?

options.C: At least 99%

why_correct: For adults with suspected sepsis, NICE advises giving oxygen to a target saturation of 94–98%, reserving the lower 88–92% range for people at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure. She has no such risk, so she should be given oxygen to reach 94–98%. Source: NICE NG253, Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over, 2025, updated 2026 (recommendation 1.10.1); BTS emergency oxygen guideline.
why_wrong: A. 88–92% is for people at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, such as some with COPD, and she has no such risk. C. Aiming for 99% or more is unnecessary, as excess oxygen gives no benefit and may cause harm. D. 80–85% is significant hypoxaemia and is unsafe as a target. E. 90–94% falls below the standard range and would leave her under-oxygenated.
pearl: Ask one question before choosing a target: is this patient at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure?
thinking: Sepsis with hypoxaemia  ↓  no COPD, neuromuscular or chest wall disease  ↓  no risk of hypercapnia  ↓  standard adult target  ↓  94–98%
exam_trap: A, 88–92% — the low target feels cautious, but it is only for people at risk of CO₂ retention.
takeaway: Most acutely ill adults need oxygen to 94–98%; use 88–92% only when hypercapnia is a risk.
notes: New vignette (pyelonephritis). The saturation targets are core PLAB figures (kept under the three-tier rule) and are stable BTS/NICE values, not a movable dose band. NG253 rec 1.10.1 applies to people 18 or over, so patient is 41.

stem:
A 67-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with a hot, swollen right knee after several days of feeling unwell. He is drowsy, his systolic blood pressure is 84 mmHg, heart rate 124 beats per minute, and his hands are cool with a slow capillary refill. Sepsis from septic arthritis is suspected, cultures have been taken, and he has no heart failure or other reason to limit fluids.

Which approach to his intravenous fluids is most appropriate?

options.A: Human albumin 4.5% as the first-choice resuscitation fluid
options.B: A bolus of 5% glucose to raise his blood pressure
options.C: One litre of crystalloid run slowly over 8 hours
options.D: A small crystalloid bolus, reassessing before more
options.E: A peripheral vasopressor started before any fluid is given

correct_answer: D. A small crystalloid bolus, reassessing before more
why_correct: Current NICE guidance is to give an isotonic crystalloid (ideally a balanced solution such as Hartmann's) as a small, rapid bolus, reassess the patient after each bolus, and repeat if needed. Currently that means 250 mL over 10–15 minutes, up to 1 litre in total, with senior advice if he has not improved by then. Source: NICE NG253, Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over, 2025, updated 2026.
why_wrong: A. Albumin is not the first-line resuscitation fluid; a crystalloid is recommended. B. 5% glucose is not a resuscitation fluid, as it distributes throughout body water and does little to restore circulating volume. C. A slow infusion over hours does not treat hypoperfusion and delays reassessment. E. Vasopressors are considered only when fluid resuscitation is not working, not before fluids have been tried.
pearl: In sepsis, fluid is given in small, quick boluses with reassessment after each one, not as one large or slow volume.
thinking: Suspected sepsis  ↓  hypotension and poor perfusion  ↓  no reason to restrict fluids  ↓  crystalloid bolus given quickly  ↓  reassess before giving more
exam_trap: C, one litre over 8 hours — it sounds like a generous volume, but a slow infusion does not correct shock and skips reassessment.
takeaway: Sepsis with poor perfusion: small rapid crystalloid boluses, reassessing after each.
notes: Re-angled so the key tests the principle (small crystalloid bolus with reassessment) rather than recall of the exact bolus volume, which is a movable guideline figure (NICE changed it from 500 mL to 250 mL in 2025). The current volume is given in the explanation only. Verified against NG253 recs 1.8.4–1.8.9 and 1.8.11–1.8.13.

stem:
A 47-year-old man is admitted to a surgical ward for a planned hernia repair, which is postponed. He usually drinks a bottle of vodka every day but has not had a drink since arriving the previous morning. The next day he has a single generalised tonic–clonic seizure lasting about a minute and recovers fully. He is not confused, has no fever, neck stiffness or focal neurological signs, and his capillary glucose is normal.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Delirium tremens
options.B: Wernicke's encephalopathy
options.C: First unprovoked epileptic seizure
options.D: Hepatic encephalopathy
options.E: Alcohol withdrawal seizure

correct_answer: E. Alcohol withdrawal seizure
why_correct: A generalised seizure about a day after a heavy, dependent drinker abruptly stops alcohol is typical of an alcohol withdrawal seizure, which usually occurs early in withdrawal. He needs a reducing benzodiazepine regimen such as chlordiazepoxide and parenteral thiamine (for example Pabrinex), with monitoring for progression to delirium tremens. Source: NICE CG100, Alcohol-use disorders: physical complications, 2010 (updated 2017).
why_wrong: A. Delirium tremens usually appears later, at around 2–3 days, with confusion, hallucinations and autonomic instability, and he is not confused. B. Wernicke's encephalopathy causes confusion, ataxia and eye signs, not an isolated seizure. C. A first seizure in someone who has just stopped heavy drinking is far more likely to be provoked by withdrawal than to be unprovoked epilepsy. D. Hepatic encephalopathy causes fluctuating confusion and a flapping tremor, and is not triggered by stopping alcohol.
pearl: Alcohol withdrawal seizures cluster early, usually within the first one to two days after the last drink, before delirium tremens would be expected.
thinking: Daily heavy drinker  ↓  abrupt stop on admission  ↓  single generalised seizure about a day later  ↓  no confusion, fever or focal signs  ↓  alcohol withdrawal seizure
exam_trap: A, delirium tremens — it is part of the same withdrawal spectrum, but it comes later and is defined by confusion and autonomic instability.
takeaway: A seizure a day or so after a heavy drinker stops is an alcohol withdrawal seizure; treat withdrawal and give thiamine.
notes: New vignette (unplanned abstinence on admission). Timing softened to 'the next day'. Distinct from BX383 (withdrawal tremor) and P073 (management).

stem:
A 52-year-old woman who has taken diazepam for anxiety for several years is found by her daughter with a pile of empty blister packs. In the emergency department she is sleepy but opens her eyes to voice and is protecting her airway. Her respiratory rate is 14 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 97% on air, pupils are normal in size, and her ECG is normal. Paracetamol and salicylate are not detected in her blood.

What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Intravenous flumazenil to reverse the sedation
options.B: Supportive care with close observation
options.C: Intravenous naloxone given in repeated doses
options.D: Gastric lavage followed by activated charcoal
options.E: An intravenous sodium bicarbonate infusion

correct_answer: B. Supportive care with close observation
why_correct: Benzodiazepine overdose on its own is usually managed supportively, with airway care, monitoring of conscious level and breathing, and observation until she wakes. Flumazenil is not used routinely, especially in long-term benzodiazepine users, because it can precipitate acute withdrawal and seizures; it is reserved for specific situations on specialist advice. Source: BNF, Poisoning, emergency treatment; TOXBASE (UK National Poisons Information Service).
why_wrong: A. Flumazenil can trigger withdrawal seizures in a long-term diazepam user and is not needed when she is breathing adequately. C. Naloxone reverses opioids, and there are no opioid features such as pinpoint pupils or slow breathing. D. Gastric lavage is not recommended, and charcoal is unsafe in a drowsy patient and of little benefit this late. E. Sodium bicarbonate is used for tricyclic cardiotoxicity, and her ECG is normal.
pearl: A drowsy patient who is breathing adequately after a benzodiazepine overdose needs observation and support, not a reversal agent.
thinking: Benzodiazepine overdose  ↓  rousable, airway protected, breathing adequately  ↓  long-term user at risk of withdrawal  ↓  no need for reversal  ↓  supportive care and observation
exam_trap: A, flumazenil — it is the specific antagonist, but in a long-term user it can provoke seizures and is unnecessary when breathing is adequate.
takeaway: Benzodiazepine overdose: support and observe; flumazenil is not routine.
notes: New vignette with a long-term user (strengthens the flumazenil-seizure safety point) and co-ingestion screen negative. Distinct from BX275 (which asks for the specific antagonist by name).

stem:
A 29-year-old man with severe toothache took paracetamol tablets repeatedly from yesterday afternoon through the night, far more than the packet allows, together with ibuprofen. He did not intend to harm himself. He now feels nauseated but otherwise well. Because the tablets were taken over many hours, there is no single time of ingestion.

Which treatment reduces his risk of liver damage?

options.A: Desferrioxamine
options.B: Acetylcysteine
options.C: Naloxone
options.D: Vitamin K
options.E: Activated charcoal

correct_answer: B. Acetylcysteine
why_correct: Acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione, which detoxifies the harmful paracetamol metabolite and so protects the liver. In a staggered overdose the treatment nomogram cannot be used, so acetylcysteine is started promptly according to the amount taken while blood tests (paracetamol concentration, liver function, INR and renal function) are sent. Source: MHRA, Paracetamol overdose: simplification of the use of intravenous acetylcysteine, 2012; TOXBASE.
why_wrong: A. Desferrioxamine is a chelator used for iron poisoning, not paracetamol. C. Naloxone reverses opioids and does not protect the liver. D. Vitamin K corrects a raised INR from warfarin, but does not prevent paracetamol liver injury. E. Activated charcoal only helps within about an hour of ingestion and cannot remove paracetamol absorbed hours earlier.
pearl: In a staggered paracetamol overdose, do not wait for a level to plot; start acetylcysteine and send bloods.
thinking: Repeated paracetamol over many hours  ↓  staggered overdose; nomogram cannot be used  ↓  toxic metabolite depletes glutathione  ↓  replenish glutathione  ↓  acetylcysteine
exam_trap: E, activated charcoal — it reduces absorption of many poisons, but only soon after a single ingestion, not after tablets taken over many hours.
takeaway: Paracetamol overdose antidote is acetylcysteine, started without waiting for a level when ingestion is staggered.
notes: Re-angled to an unintentional staggered overdose so it does not repeat the single-ingestion nomogram questions (CR045, GAS012, CP010, NEP031). Same key (acetylcysteine). Thresholds softened into words (no mg/kg band).

stem:
A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after being found with his grandmother's amitriptyline tablets, several of which are missing. He is drowsy and irritable, with dilated pupils, flushed dry skin and a heart rate of 170 beats per minute. His ECG shows a broad-complex tachycardia, and a blood gas shows a metabolic acidosis.

Which treatment should be given for his cardiotoxicity?

options.A: Flumazenil
options.B: Amiodarone
options.C: Naloxone hydrochloride
options.D: Sodium bicarbonate
options.E: Acetylcysteine

correct_answer: D. Sodium bicarbonate
why_correct: Tricyclic antidepressants block cardiac sodium channels, widening the QRS and causing arrhythmias, made worse by acidosis. Intravenous sodium bicarbonate counters this by alkalinising the blood and providing a sodium load, and is given for QRS widening, arrhythmias, hypotension or acidosis, with advice from TOXBASE or the National Poisons Information Service. Source: TOXBASE (UK National Poisons Information Service); BNF, Poisoning, emergency treatment.
why_wrong: A. Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines and can provoke seizures in tricyclic poisoning. B. Amiodarone can worsen tricyclic cardiotoxicity and is avoided; arrhythmias are treated with bicarbonate first. C. Naloxone reverses opioids and does not treat sodium-channel blockade. E. Acetylcysteine is the antidote for paracetamol, not tricyclics.
pearl: Even a few adult-strength tricyclic tablets can be dangerous to a small child; a broad QRS means sodium-channel toxicity.
thinking: Toddler has taken amitriptyline  ↓  anticholinergic features and drowsiness  ↓  broad QRS and acidosis  ↓  sodium-channel blockade  ↓  intravenous sodium bicarbonate
exam_trap: B, amiodarone — it is a standard drug for broad-complex tachycardia, but in tricyclic poisoning it can worsen toxicity; bicarbonate comes first.
takeaway: Tricyclic poisoning with a broad QRS: give IV sodium bicarbonate.
notes: Re-angled to accidental paediatric ingestion because the adult deliberate-overdose scenario already exists (CP011, adult amitriptyline with broad QRS and seizure, key IV sodium bicarbonate). Same learning point and key. Amiodarone added as a distractor (avoided in TCA poisoning per TOXBASE/BNF).

stem:
A 31-year-old woman comes to the emergency department after two nights in a static caravan heated by an old gas fire. She has a throbbing headache, nausea and light-headedness, and her partner, who stayed with her, has the same symptoms. They both felt a little better during the drive to hospital. Her pulse oximeter reads 99% on air.

How should the oximeter reading be interpreted?

options.A: It rules out any significant carbon monoxide exposure
options.B: It confirms a viral illness shared by the couple
options.C: It shows that oxygen therapy is not required
options.D: It may be falsely normal despite carbon monoxide
options.E: It suggests the symptoms are due to anxiety

correct_answer: D. It may be falsely normal despite carbon monoxide
why_correct: Standard pulse oximeters cannot tell carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin, so saturations can read normal even in significant carbon monoxide poisoning. Shared symptoms in people using the same fuel-burning appliance, improving away from it, strongly suggest exposure; measure carboxyhaemoglobin on a blood gas and give high-flow oxygen through a non-rebreathe mask without waiting for the result. Source: UKHSA, Carbon monoxide: health effects and management, 2024; NICE CKS, Carbon monoxide poisoning.
why_wrong: A. Pulse oximetry reads carboxyhaemoglobin as oxyhaemoglobin, so a normal reading cannot exclude exposure. B. A shared illness linked to a gas appliance, easing away from it, points to poisoning rather than a virus. C. High-flow oxygen is the treatment for suspected carbon monoxide poisoning regardless of the oximeter reading. E. Anxiety does not explain the same symptoms in two people sharing a gas-heated space.
pearl: Headache in more than one person sharing a space with a fuel-burning appliance is carbon monoxide until proved otherwise, whatever the oximeter says.
thinking: Old gas fire in an enclosed caravan  ↓  headache and nausea in two people, easing away from it  ↓  oximeter cannot detect carboxyhaemoglobin  ↓  normal reading is falsely reassuring  ↓  measure carboxyhaemoglobin and give high-flow oxygen
exam_trap: A, it excludes carbon monoxide — a normal oximeter is usually reassuring, but here it misreads carboxyhaemoglobin as oxygenated blood.
takeaway: A normal pulse oximeter never excludes carbon monoxide poisoning.
notes: New scenario (caravan, two people). Distinct learning point from ACU045/NEU045/CP032 (treatment) and BX688 (which poison to suspect).

stem:
A 26-year-old man with known epilepsy has a generalised tonic–clonic seizure in the emergency department waiting room. The jerking stops briefly, but before he opens his eyes or responds to voice, a second convulsion begins. Staff place him on his side and give oxygen, and his capillary glucose is normal.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Convulsive syncope
options.B: Convulsive status epilepticus
options.C: Post-ictal confusional state
options.D: Panic attack with hyperventilation
options.E: Transient ischaemic attack

correct_answer: B. Convulsive status epilepticus
why_correct: Recurrent seizures without recovery of consciousness between them meet the definition of convulsive status epilepticus, as does a single convulsion lasting 5 minutes or more. It is a medical emergency: secure the airway, give oxygen, check glucose and give a benzodiazepine promptly (buccal midazolam or IV lorazepam), because seizures become harder to stop the longer they last. Source: NICE NG217, Epilepsies in children, young people and adults, 2022.
why_wrong: A. Convulsive syncope causes a few brief jerks with rapid recovery once flat, not repeated convulsions. C. A post-ictal state follows a seizure that has ended, whereas his convulsions are recurring. D. A panic attack does not cause convulsions with loss of awareness. E. A transient ischaemic attack causes brief focal deficits, not generalised convulsions.
pearl: Status epilepticus is defined both by duration and by seizures that recur before consciousness returns.
thinking: Generalised convulsion  ↓  second seizure begins before he regains awareness  ↓  no recovery between seizures  ↓  convulsive status epilepticus  ↓  emergency benzodiazepine treatment
exam_trap: C, post-ictal confusional state — not waking after a seizure is expected, but a fresh convulsion before recovery makes this status epilepticus.
takeaway: Seizures that recur without recovery in between are status epilepticus: treat immediately.
notes: New vignette; the key turns on the definition (recurrence without recovery) rather than a time threshold. NG217 definition used.

stem:
A 36-year-old woman is stung by a wasp while gardening and develops wheeze, lip swelling and low blood pressure. A paramedic gives one dose of intramuscular adrenaline, and a second dose is needed in the emergency department, after which she recovers completely. An hour later she feels well, her observations are normal and she asks to go home to her children.

What is the most appropriate plan?

options.A: Discharge now with a short course of oral prednisolone
options.B: Discharge now if a mast cell tryptase level is normal
options.C: Keep her under observation for several more hours
options.D: Give a further dose of IM adrenaline, then discharge
options.E: Discharge now with oral antihistamine and GP follow-up

correct_answer: C. Keep her under observation for several more hours
why_correct: Anaphylaxis can recur after apparent recovery, and the length of observation depends on severity. Because she needed two doses of adrenaline, Resuscitation Council UK advises observation for at least 6 hours after her symptoms resolved. Before discharge she needs senior review, two adrenaline auto-injectors with training, written advice and referral to an allergy clinic. Source: Resuscitation Council UK, Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis, 2021.
why_wrong: A. Steroids are not recommended routinely and do not reliably prevent a recurrence, so they cannot replace observation. B. Mast cell tryptase helps confirm the diagnosis later, but a normal result does not make early discharge safe. D. Adrenaline is not given prophylactically to someone who is well. E. Antihistamines treat skin symptoms but do not prevent a recurrence.
pearl: The more adrenaline a reaction needed, the longer the observation period before discharge.
thinking: Wasp-sting anaphylaxis  ↓  two doses of adrenaline needed  ↓  now well  ↓  recurrence still possible  ↓  observe for several hours before discharge
exam_trap: E, oral antihistamine and discharge — she looks completely well, but a reaction needing two adrenaline doses requires a longer observation period.
takeaway: After anaphylaxis, observe for a period guided by severity because symptoms can return.
notes: New vignette; severity (two adrenaline doses) drives the observation period. Key avoids hinging on the exact hours; figures given in the explanation are from RCUK 2021 (verified in the PDF table). Distinct from BX689 (naming biphasic reaction) and from PAN2910 (reason for observation after a single dose).

stem:
A 63-year-old man with type 2 diabetes treated with insulin is brought to the emergency department after a seizure at a bus stop. Twenty minutes later he is still unresponsive to voice, with snoring breathing that improves with a jaw thrust. An intravenous cannula has already been placed, and his capillary glucose is 1.9 mmol/L.

What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.A: Glucose gel squeezed between his gum and cheek
options.B: A sugary drink once his airway has been supported
options.C: Observe as post-ictal and recheck glucose in 15 minutes
options.D: Intravenous glucose given immediately
options.E: A variable-rate intravenous insulin infusion

correct_answer: D. Intravenous glucose given immediately
why_correct: His seizure and failure to wake are explained by severe hypoglycaemia, and he cannot protect his airway, so nothing should be given by mouth. With IV access available, give IV glucose (10% or 20%) and recheck the glucose about 10 minutes later; IM glucagon is the alternative only when there is no IV access. Once he is awake and able to swallow, he needs a longer-acting carbohydrate and review of his insulin. Source: JBDS-IP, The hospital management of hypoglycaemia in adults with diabetes mellitus, 2023.
why_wrong: A. Glucose gel is unsafe in a patient who cannot protect his airway, because of aspiration risk. B. Oral fluids must not be given to someone who is unresponsive. C. Treating the coma as simply post-ictal delays correction of a dangerously low glucose. E. Insulin would lower his glucose further.
pearl: Always check glucose in anyone who has had a seizure or is not waking up; hypoglycaemia is quick to fix and dangerous to miss.
thinking: Insulin-treated diabetes  ↓  seizure and still unresponsive  ↓  glucose 1.9 mmol/L  ↓  cannot swallow safely, so nothing by mouth  ↓  IV glucose via the cannula
exam_trap: C, post-ictal state — not waking after a seizure seems expected, but here the low glucose is the cause and needs treating now.
takeaway: Unconscious hypoglycaemia: IV glucose if access is available, IM glucagon if not; never oral.
notes: Re-angled to hypoglycaemia presenting as a seizure with a post-ictal trap. Learning point overlaps ACU023/END003/END010 (route of glucose when unable to swallow), but the scenario differs (seizure/post-ictal presentation, airway manoeuvre). Reviewer may judge overlap.

stem:
A 34-year-old man has a travel vaccine injected into his upper arm by the practice nurse at his GP surgery. Within a minute he says he feels faint, then slumps in the chair, looking pale and clammy. His pulse is slow at 48 beats per minute. He is laid flat with his legs raised and is fully alert again within a minute, with a good-volume pulse. His skin shows no rash or swelling, his breathing is quiet and his chest is clear.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Anaphylactic reaction to the vaccine
options.B: Hypoglycaemic episode
options.C: Generalised tonic–clonic seizure
options.D: Panic attack with hyperventilation
options.E: Vasovagal syncope

correct_answer: E. Vasovagal syncope
why_correct: Fainting within seconds to a minute of an injection, with pallor, clamminess and a slow pulse, and rapid recovery when lying flat, is a vasovagal reaction. Anaphylaxis usually develops over minutes with a fast, weak pulse, skin or mucosal changes and airway or breathing problems, and it does not settle simply by lying down. Source: UKHSA, Immunisation against infectious disease (Green Book), chapter 8, 2023; Resuscitation Council UK, Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis, 2021.
why_wrong: A. Anaphylaxis causes a fast pulse with airway, breathing or skin features, none of which are present, and it does not resolve on lying flat. B. Hypoglycaemia does not cause instant collapse at injection with full recovery within a minute. C. There was no convulsion, and recovery was immediate without post-ictal confusion. D. A panic attack causes rapid breathing and a fast pulse, not a slow pulse with collapse.
pearl: A slow pulse points to a faint; a fast, weak pulse with skin or airway changes points to anaphylaxis.
thinking: Injection  ↓  pale, clammy, slumps within a minute  ↓  slow pulse  ↓  rapid recovery lying flat, no rash, wheeze or swelling  ↓  vasovagal syncope
exam_trap: A, anaphylaxis — any collapse after a vaccine prompts it, but the slow pulse, quick recovery supine and absent skin or airway signs fit a faint.
takeaway: Collapse at injection with a slow pulse and rapid recovery lying flat is a vasovagal faint, not anaphylaxis.
notes: Checker C2: patient changed from a 17-year-old student to an adult man at a GP surgery to separate it from BX020 (student fainting at a vaccination). New vignette; bradycardia is the key discriminator from anaphylaxis (Green Book ch.8).

stem:
A frail 78-year-old woman of low body weight has had severe back pain for 4 days. Her daughter finds that she has been taking paracetamol tablets much more often than the label allows, as well as hot cold-and-flu drinks that also contain paracetamol. She had no intention of harming herself and feels well apart from her back pain.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Urgent assessment with paracetamol level and liver tests
options.B: Reassure her, as she has no symptoms of liver injury
options.C: Advise her to stop paracetamol and see her GP next week
options.D: Give activated charcoal and allow her home with her daughter
options.E: Switch her to co-codamol and recheck liver tests in a month

correct_answer: A. Urgent assessment with paracetamol level and liver tests
why_correct: Repeated supratherapeutic paracetamol use (therapeutic excess) can cause serious liver injury while the person still feels well, and low body weight increases the risk. She needs urgent hospital assessment following the paracetamol poisoning pathway, with blood tests including paracetamol concentration, liver function, INR and renal function, and acetylcysteine if indicated; the treatment nomogram cannot be used for this pattern. Source: TOXBASE (UK National Poisons Information Service); MHRA, Paracetamol overdose: simplification of the use of intravenous acetylcysteine, 2012.
why_wrong: B. Liver injury from paracetamol is often silent early, so feeling well does not mean she is safe. C. Waiting a week could miss the window when acetylcysteine is most effective. D. Charcoal has no role after repeated doses over several days and does not replace assessment. E. Co-codamol still contains paracetamol, and delaying tests risks missing liver injury.
pearl: Therapeutic excess counts as paracetamol poisoning even when the intent was only pain relief.
thinking: Repeated excess paracetamol over days  ↓  hidden extra paracetamol in cold remedies  ↓  low body weight raises risk  ↓  silent early liver injury  ↓  urgent bloods and the poisoning pathway
exam_trap: B, reassurance because she feels well — paracetamol toxicity is often silent until liver damage is established.
takeaway: Feeling well never rules out paracetamol toxicity: assess with bloods and follow the poisoning pathway.
notes: Re-angled to unintentional therapeutic excess in an older woman because the deliberate single-overdose 'feels well' scenario duplicates BX387 (and ACU019/NEP031). Same learning point (an asymptomatic patient still needs the paracetamol poisoning pathway). Doses softened into words.

stem:
A 38-year-old engineer is caught by a burst high-pressure steam pipe in a small plant room. He has scald burns to his face and neck and says his throat feels raw and painful to swallow. On arrival his oxygen saturation is 97% on air and he is talking, but over the next half hour his voice becomes increasingly hoarse.

What is the most important immediate concern?

options.A: Infection of the facial burns
options.B: Fluid loss from the burned skin
options.C: Progressive swelling of the upper airway
options.D: Corneal injury from heat exposure
options.E: Scarring and contracture of the neck skin

correct_answer: C. Progressive swelling of the upper airway
why_correct: Steam carries far more heat than dry hot air and can burn the larynx and even the airway below it. A sore throat, painful swallowing and a voice that is becoming hoarse signal developing oedema, which can obstruct the airway over the next hours even though he is talking and saturating well now. He needs urgent senior anaesthetic review for early airway assessment and possible intubation, before swelling makes this more difficult. Source: NICE CKS, Burns and scalds, 2024.
why_wrong: A. Burn infection is a later complication, not the immediate threat. B. Fluid loss matters in large burns, but a facial and neck burn of this size is not the first priority. D. Eye injury should be checked, but it does not threaten life. E. Scarring is a long-term problem that does not affect immediate survival.
pearl: A changing voice after a thermal injury to the face or throat means the airway is swelling; normal saturations do not mean the airway is safe.
thinking: Steam injury in an enclosed space  ↓  face and neck scalds with a painful throat  ↓  voice becoming hoarse  ↓  laryngeal oedema developing  ↓  progressive upper airway obstruction
exam_trap: B, fluid loss from the burns — fluid resuscitation is a burns priority, but here the airway is swelling and is the immediate threat.
takeaway: Hoarseness after a heat injury to the face or throat means an airway at risk: involve anaesthetics early.
notes: Re-angled to a steam (thermal) airway injury because the house-fire soot/hoarseness scenario is already covered twice (ACU034, BX687). Same learning point and key (developing airway obstruction from inhalational/thermal injury). CKS not fetchable by curl (JS); statements are standard burns airway teaching.

stem:
A 69-year-old man is helped out of his flat by firefighters after a pan caught fire and filled his kitchen with smoke; he has no burns. Thirty minutes later he has a pounding headache, has vomited twice and is slow to answer questions. His blood pressure and heart rate are normal, his pupils are equal and reactive, and pulse oximetry reads 99% on air.

Which poisoning best explains his symptoms?

options.A: Organophosphate insecticide poisoning
options.B: Opioid poisoning
options.C: Cyanide poisoning
options.D: Carbon monoxide poisoning
options.E: Salicylate poisoning

correct_answer: D. Carbon monoxide poisoning
why_correct: Carbon monoxide is the commonest poison after smoke exposure and causes headache, vomiting and confusion, while standard pulse oximetry reads normal because it cannot tell carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin. Measure carboxyhaemoglobin on a blood gas and give high-flow oxygen through a non-rebreathe mask straight away. Source: UKHSA, Carbon monoxide: health effects and management, 2024.
why_wrong: A. Organophosphates cause sweating, salivation, small pupils and a slow pulse, and are not a feature of a kitchen fire. B. Opioid poisoning causes pinpoint pupils and slow breathing, which he does not have. C. Cyanide can occur in smoke from burning plastics and furnishings, but it typically causes collapse, low blood pressure and severe lactic acidosis, not this milder picture. E. Salicylate poisoning causes tinnitus and fast breathing and is unrelated to smoke.
pearl: After smoke exposure, suspect carbon monoxide first; suspect cyanide as well when there is collapse, shock or a severe lactic acidosis.
thinking: Smoke exposure in an enclosed kitchen  ↓  headache, vomiting and slowed thinking  ↓  stable circulation, normal pupils  ↓  oximetry falsely normal  ↓  carbon monoxide poisoning
exam_trap: C, cyanide — it is a real risk in fires, but it causes collapse, shock and severe acidosis; a stable patient with headache and vomiting fits carbon monoxide.
takeaway: Smoke exposure with headache and confusion but normal saturations: think carbon monoxide and give high-flow oxygen.
notes: New scenario (kitchen fire, single older man). The source's 'cyanide only' option (key-by-absurdity) replaced with a fair cyanide distractor discriminated by haemodynamics/acidosis (consistent with NEP036). Distinct from NEU045 (treatment) and BX688 (boiler).

stem:
A 45-year-old man is struck by lightning while sheltering under a tree on a golf course. Friends find him dazed on the ground; he has a fern-like red pattern on his chest, ringing in his ears and tingling in both legs, but he is breathing and talking. He is brought to the emergency department.

Which complication is it most important to assess for now?

options.A: Delayed cataract formation
options.B: Primary hypothyroidism
options.C: Rupture of the eardrum
options.D: Acute pancreatitis
options.E: Cardiac arrhythmia

correct_answer: E. Cardiac arrhythmia
why_correct: Lightning and other electrical injuries can disrupt the heart's conduction, causing arrhythmias that range from minor changes to cardiac arrest, so he needs an ECG and cardiac monitoring. The visible skin marks often underestimate the internal injury. Source: Resuscitation Council UK / ERC Guidelines 2021, Cardiac arrest in special circumstances (electrocution and lightning).
why_wrong: A. Cataracts are a recognised late effect of lightning injury, but they develop over months and are not the immediate threat. B. Hypothyroidism is not a complication of lightning or electrical injury. C. Eardrum rupture is common after lightning and should be checked, but it is not life-threatening. D. Pancreatitis is not an expected complication of lightning strike.
pearl: The fern-like (Lichtenberg) skin pattern is characteristic of lightning, and the heart is the organ most at immediate risk.
thinking: Lightning strike  ↓  current passes through the body  ↓  interferes with cardiac conduction  ↓  risk of arrhythmia or arrest  ↓  ECG and monitoring
exam_trap: C, eardrum rupture — it is common after lightning and fits his ringing ears, but it is not life-threatening; the heart is.
takeaway: After lightning or electrical injury, check the ECG and monitor for arrhythmia.
notes: Re-angled to lightning strike because the electrical-shock-at-work scenario with the same key duplicates BX413 (factory worker, small hand burn, key cardiac arrhythmia). Same learning point and key. The source's 'cataract formation only' absurd option replaced with a fair 'delayed cataract' distractor.

stem:
A 58-year-old man was eating steak at a restaurant when he felt a piece stick behind his lower breastbone. Two hours later he is spitting into a bowl because he cannot swallow even his own saliva. He is breathing comfortably and talking normally.

What does his inability to swallow saliva indicate?

options.A: Oesophageal spasm likely to settle on its own
options.B: Complete obstruction of the oesophagus
options.C: Obstruction at the gastric outlet
options.D: A foreign body lodged in the larynx
options.E: Anxiety-related globus sensation

correct_answer: B. Complete obstruction of the oesophagus
why_correct: A food bolus that stops a person swallowing even saliva is completely blocking the oesophagus. This carries a risk of aspiration and of oesophageal injury, so it needs urgent endoscopy, ideally within a few hours, rather than a wait for it to pass; an underlying stricture, cancer or eosinophilic oesophagitis should be looked for. Source: ESGE guideline, Removal of foreign bodies in the upper gastrointestinal tract in adults, 2016.
why_wrong: A. Spasm would not cause constant inability to swallow saliva after a clear food-impaction event, and waiting risks complications. C. Gastric outlet obstruction causes vomiting after meals, not sudden inability to swallow saliva. D. A laryngeal foreign body would cause choking, stridor or voice change, and he is breathing and talking normally. E. Globus is a sensation of a lump without true obstruction, and patients can still swallow.
pearl: Inability to swallow saliva separates complete from partial food bolus obstruction and raises the urgency of endoscopy.
thinking: Meat sticks behind the sternum  ↓  cannot swallow even saliva  ↓  nothing can pass the bolus  ↓  complete oesophageal obstruction  ↓  urgent endoscopy
exam_trap: A, oesophageal spasm likely to settle — many boluses do pass, but total inability to swallow saliva means complete obstruction that should not be left.
takeaway: Food bolus with inability to swallow saliva means complete oesophageal obstruction needing urgent endoscopy.
notes: New vignette. ESGE (2016) is the guideline UK endoscopists follow: emergency endoscopy within 6 hours for complete oesophageal obstruction (softened to 'within a few hours'). No duplicate found (GAS110 is EoE diagnosis).

stem:
A 24-year-old man with a known peanut allergy accidentally eats a curry containing groundnuts and develops throat tightness, wheeze and widespread hives. A single dose of intramuscular adrenaline in the emergency department brings rapid and complete recovery. Thirty minutes afterwards he feels back to normal, and his wife asks why he cannot leave straight away.

What is the main reason for keeping him under observation?

options.A: The adrenaline may cause a delayed surge in blood pressure
options.B: Symptoms may return hours later without further exposure
options.C: He is likely to develop asthma over the next few days
options.D: Delayed infection commonly follows food allergy reactions
options.E: His kidneys are often injured after severe allergic reactions

correct_answer: B. Symptoms may return hours later without further exposure
why_correct: After apparent recovery from anaphylaxis, symptoms can return hours later without any further allergen exposure (a biphasic reaction), and no reliable test predicts who will be affected. A period of observation in hospital is therefore needed; after a rapid response to a single dose, discharge may be considered after a shorter period if he has adrenaline auto-injectors, has been trained to use them and will be supervised. Source: Resuscitation Council UK, Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis, 2021.
why_wrong: A. Adrenaline has a short duration of action, and a delayed rise in blood pressure is not the reason for observation. C. Anaphylaxis does not cause asthma, although asthma is a risk factor for severe reactions. D. Food allergy reactions are not followed by delayed infection. E. Kidney injury is not a usual consequence of anaphylaxis that resolves promptly.
