pearl: A biphasic reaction can follow even a mild-looking, quickly treated episode, so observe and give auto-injectors and allergy referral before discharge.
thinking: Anaphylaxis after peanut  ↓  rapid recovery after one adrenaline dose  ↓  recurrence possible hours later without re-exposure  ↓  biphasic reaction  ↓  observe before discharge
exam_trap: A, delayed surge in blood pressure — adrenaline side effects are real but brief; the reason for observation is a returning reaction.
takeaway: Anaphylaxis can recur hours later without re-exposure: observe before discharge.
notes: New vignette (food anaphylaxis, single dose). Distinct from PAN275 (management when two doses needed) and BX689 (naming biphasic recurrence that has occurred). Observation guidance verified in RCUK 2021 table.

stem:
A 29-year-old woman wakes up with a markedly swollen upper lip and puffy eyelids that were not there when she went to bed. The swelling feels tight rather than itchy, the overlying skin is a normal colour, and she has no fever, pain or wheals anywhere else. She can speak, swallow and breathe normally.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Cellulitis of the face
options.B: Contact dermatitis
options.C: Allergic conjunctivitis
options.D: Angioedema
options.E: Orbital cellulitis

correct_answer: D. Angioedema
why_correct: Sudden, non-pitting swelling of loose tissues such as the lips and eyelids, with normal-coloured skin and no surface rash, is angioedema, caused by swelling in the deeper dermis and submucosa. Check for tongue or throat involvement and breathing difficulty, ask about ACE inhibitors and other triggers, and consider hereditary or acquired causes if it recurs without urticaria. Source: NICE CKS, Angio-oedema and anaphylaxis, 2024.
why_wrong: A. Facial cellulitis is usually one-sided, red, hot and painful, often with fever. B. Contact dermatitis causes an itchy, red, scaly or weeping rash at the contact site. C. Allergic conjunctivitis causes red, itchy, watery eyes rather than lip swelling. E. Orbital cellulitis causes a painful, red, swollen eye with fever and often reduced eye movement or vision.
pearl: Normal-coloured, non-itchy swelling of the lips or eyelids points to angioedema; always ask about ACE inhibitors and check the airway.
thinking: Overnight swelling of lip and eyelids  ↓  tight, not itchy; normal skin colour  ↓  no fever, pain or rash  ↓  deep dermal and submucosal swelling  ↓  angioedema
exam_trap: A, cellulitis of the face — it causes facial swelling, but with redness, heat, pain and usually fever.
takeaway: Sudden lip and eyelid swelling without rash or inflammation is angioedema: assess the airway and look for the cause.
notes: New vignette with no medication history, so the item tests recognition (DER039/DER006 test ACE-inhibitor cause and action).

stem:
A 10-year-old boy with type 1 diabetes collapses during a school football match. When the ambulance crew arrive he is unresponsive but breathing, and his capillary glucose is 1.7 mmol/L. They have not been able to gain venous access.

What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.A: Glucose gel rubbed inside his cheek
options.B: Sips of a sugary drink through a straw
options.C: Delay treatment until venous access is gained
options.D: Intramuscular glucagon injection
options.E: Buccal midazolam to prevent a seizure

correct_answer: D. Intramuscular glucagon injection
why_correct: An unconscious child cannot swallow safely, so oral glucose risks aspiration; hypoglycaemia must be treated urgently by a non-oral route. Without venous access, intramuscular glucagon is the right choice, followed by oral carbohydrate once he is awake and able to swallow, and hospital assessment. Source: BNF for Children, Glucagon; NICE NG18, Diabetes (type 1 and type 2) in children and young people, 2015 (updated 2023).
why_wrong: A. Glucose gel is for a conscious child who can swallow; it is unsafe when he is unresponsive. B. Drinks must not be given to an unconscious child because of aspiration risk. C. Waiting for IV access delays treatment of a dangerously low glucose. E. Midazolam treats seizures and does not correct the hypoglycaemia that is causing his unconsciousness.
pearl: The deciding question in hypoglycaemia is whether the person can swallow safely; if not, use IV glucose or IM glucagon.
thinking: Type 1 diabetes, exercise  ↓  unresponsive with very low glucose  ↓  cannot swallow safely  ↓  no IV access  ↓  intramuscular glucagon
exam_trap: A, glucose gel inside the cheek — it is a familiar hypoglycaemia treatment, but it needs a child who can swallow and protect the airway.
takeaway: Unconscious hypoglycaemia: treat by a non-oral route, IM glucagon if there is no IV access.
notes: Re-angled to a paediatric pre-hospital scenario so it does not repeat the adult insulin-treated scenarios (END003, END010, ACU023). Same learning point (non-oral treatment when unable to swallow). Glucagon dose deliberately not tested.

stem:
A 55-year-old woman in the emergency department with crushing central chest pain suddenly stops responding while she is being attached to the monitor. She is not breathing normally and has no carotid pulse. The monitor shows an irregular, wavy baseline of varying size with no identifiable P waves, QRS complexes or T waves.

Which rhythm is shown?

options.A: Ventricular fibrillation
options.B: Pulseless electrical activity
options.C: Asystole
options.D: Atrial fibrillation with a fast ventricular rate
options.E: Complete heart block

correct_answer: A. Ventricular fibrillation
why_correct: A chaotic, irregular waveform of varying size with no recognisable complexes in a pulseless patient is ventricular fibrillation, a common rhythm in cardiac arrest from acute myocardial ischaemia. It is shockable: start CPR and defibrillate as quickly as possible, following the Advanced Life Support algorithm. Source: Resuscitation Council UK, Adult Advanced Life Support Guidelines, 2021.
why_wrong: B. Pulseless electrical activity shows organised complexes on the monitor despite no pulse, not chaotic activity. C. Asystole is an almost flat line, not an irregular wavy trace of varying size. D. Atrial fibrillation has recognisable QRS complexes and usually a pulse. E. Complete heart block shows regular P waves and separate, regular QRS complexes.
pearl: In an arrest, organised complexes without a pulse mean PEA, while chaotic waves with no complexes mean VF.
thinking: Unresponsive, not breathing normally, no pulse  ↓  cardiac arrest  ↓  chaotic waveform, no QRS complexes  ↓  disorganised ventricular activity  ↓  ventricular fibrillation
exam_trap: B, pulseless electrical activity — it is also an arrest rhythm, but it shows organised complexes rather than chaotic waves.
takeaway: A pulseless patient with chaotic, formless ECG activity is in VF: shock early.
notes: New vignette (ED, chest pain). Distinct from CARD036 (immediate action for VF) — this item tests rhythm recognition.

stem:
During a prolonged heatwave, an 84-year-old woman who lives alone in a top-floor flat is found by a neighbour lying on her sofa, muddled and drowsy. Her skin is hot and dry, her heart rate is 118 beats per minute and her core temperature is 41°C. She has started no new medicines and has no cough, urinary symptoms or neck stiffness.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Heat exhaustion
options.B: Heatstroke
options.C: Thyroid storm
options.D: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
options.E: Serotonin syndrome

correct_answer: B. Heatstroke
why_correct: A very high core temperature with confusion or reduced consciousness in a hot environment is heatstroke, a medical emergency. Older people living alone in hot, poorly ventilated homes are at particular risk of this 'classic' form during heatwaves. She needs immediate active cooling and supportive care, while infection is still considered and excluded. Source: UKHSA, Supporting vulnerable people before and during hot weather: healthcare professionals, 2024.
why_wrong: A. Heat exhaustion causes weakness, dizziness and sweating with a less raised temperature, and the mind stays clear. C. Thyroid storm occurs in known or untreated hyperthyroidism, usually with a trigger, and there is nothing to suggest it here. D. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome follows antipsychotic use and causes marked rigidity. E. Serotonin syndrome follows serotonergic drugs and causes clonus and agitation.
pearl: The feature that separates heatstroke from heat exhaustion is central nervous system dysfunction, such as confusion, drowsiness or seizures.
thinking: Prolonged heatwave, older woman alone  ↓  hot, dry skin and very high core temperature  ↓  confused and drowsy  ↓  no drug or infective trigger  ↓  heatstroke
exam_trap: A, heat exhaustion — it shares the setting, but confusion and drowsiness signal heatstroke.
takeaway: Heat exposure with a very high temperature and altered mental state is heatstroke: cool immediately.
notes: Re-angled to classic (non-exertional) heatstroke in an older person because the exertional outdoor-worker and runner scenarios already exist (BX411, BX698, DT144, DT145). NEU046 uses a similar setting but tests treatment, not diagnosis.

stem:
A 79-year-old man is found by his carer on the kitchen floor of his unheated house, having lain there all night after a fall. He is drowsy and no longer shivering, his core temperature is 27°C, and he has a slow but palpable pulse of 36 beats per minute. The ambulance crew are about to transfer him to the stretcher.

Which principle is most important in his immediate care?

options.A: Rewarm him quickly in a hot bath
options.B: Give IV atropine to raise his heart rate
options.C: Handle gently and keep him horizontal
options.D: Sit him up and encourage him to walk
options.E: Give a warm alcoholic drink to warm him

correct_answer: C. Handle gently and keep him horizontal
why_correct: In severe hypothermia the cold heart is very irritable, and rough handling, sitting up or exertion can trigger ventricular fibrillation or collapse. He should be moved gently and kept horizontal, have wet clothing removed, be insulated, and be rewarmed in a controlled way with cardiac monitoring. Source: Resuscitation Council UK / ERC Guidelines 2021, Cardiac arrest in special circumstances (accidental hypothermia).
why_wrong: A. Rapid immersion in a hot bath can cause sudden vasodilatation, collapse and arrhythmias, so rewarming should be controlled. B. Bradycardia in hypothermia is expected, responds poorly to atropine and improves with rewarming. D. Sitting up and walking can provoke collapse and ventricular fibrillation in a severely cold patient. E. Alcohol causes peripheral vasodilatation and worsens heat loss.
pearl: A slow pulse in severe hypothermia is a physiological response to cold; treat the temperature, not the heart rate.
thinking: Long lie in a cold house  ↓  severe hypothermia with drowsiness and bradycardia  ↓  cold myocardium is irritable  ↓  jolting or exertion can trigger VF  ↓  handle gently, keep horizontal
exam_trap: B, IV atropine — treating a slow pulse seems logical, but hypothermic bradycardia is physiological and settles with rewarming.
takeaway: Severe hypothermia: handle gently, keep horizontal and rewarm in a controlled way.
notes: New vignette (long lie at home). Core temperature given as a supporting figure; key does not depend on the number. Distinct from BX695 (definition) and DS059 (arrest).

stem:
A 34-year-old hillwalker is brought to the emergency department after a night stranded on a Scottish mountain in sub-zero conditions. Several fingertips on both hands are hard, waxy-white and numb. His core temperature has now been corrected in a warm resuscitation bay and there is no chance of him returning to the cold.

Which is the most appropriate way to thaw his fingers?

options.A: Massage the fingertips vigorously to restore blood flow
options.B: Hold the hands close to a radiator until colour returns
options.C: Pack the fingers in ice until surgical review
options.D: Immerse the hands in a circulating warm-water bath
options.E: Puncture and drain any blisters before thawing

correct_answer: D. Immerse the hands in a circulating warm-water bath
why_correct: Once any hypothermia has been treated and there is no risk of refreezing, frozen tissue should be thawed rapidly by immersion in warm (not hot), circulating water, with strong analgesia because rewarming is very painful. Rapid controlled rewarming limits ongoing ice-crystal damage, whereas friction and uncontrolled heat increase tissue loss. Source: NHS 'Frostbite', accessed 2026; Wilderness Medical Society frostbite clinical practice guideline, 2024 update.
why_wrong: A. Rubbing frozen tissue causes mechanical damage to fragile, ice-laden cells and must be avoided. B. Dry heat from a radiator cannot be controlled and readily burns numb, insensate skin. C. Applying ice prolongs freezing and extends tissue loss. E. Blisters are not routinely drained before rewarming; their handling is a later specialist decision.
pearl: Thaw frostbite only when refreezing cannot happen, using rapid warm-water immersion with good analgesia, and never rub the tissue or use direct dry heat.
thinking: Hard, white, numb fingertips after cold exposure  ↓  Frostbite; hypothermia corrected and no refreezing risk  ↓  Thaw rapidly but in a controlled way  ↓  Avoid friction, dry heat and ice  ↓  Warm-water bath immersion with analgesia
exam_trap: B appeals because warmth seems logical, but a radiator gives uncontrolled dry heat that burns numb tissue.
takeaway: Frostbite is thawed by rapid, controlled warm-water immersion once refreezing is impossible.
notes: New vignette (named setting, corrected hypothermia made explicit, since rewarming of frostbite follows correction of core temperature). Key unchanged. Water temperature figure deliberately omitted (rule 1). Distractors reworded/reordered.

stem:
A lifeguard pulls a 12-year-old girl from the sea after she is seen floating face-down. On the sand she is unresponsive and making only occasional gasping movements. A bystander has already called 999.

What should the lifeguard do first?

options.A: Open the airway, give five rescue breaths, then CPR
options.B: Turn her into the recovery position and keep her warm
options.C: Use abdominal thrusts to expel water from her lungs
options.D: Wait for the ambulance crew before starting treatment
options.E: Start chest compressions only, without rescue breaths

correct_answer: A. Open the airway, give five rescue breaths, then CPR
why_correct: Occasional gasping is not normal breathing, so she is in cardiac arrest, and arrest after drowning is caused primarily by hypoxia. UK resuscitation guidance for drowning (and for children generally) is to open the airway and give five initial rescue breaths before starting chest compressions, because restoring oxygenation is the priority. Source: Resuscitation Council UK, Special Circumstances and Paediatric Basic Life Support guidelines, 2021.
why_wrong: B. The recovery position is for an unresponsive patient who is breathing normally, and agonal gasping is a sign of cardiac arrest. C. Abdominal thrusts to drain water delay ventilation and risk vomiting and aspiration. D. Waiting for the ambulance wastes the minutes in which a hypoxic arrest may still be reversible. E. Compression-only CPR omits ventilation, which is the core treatment for a hypoxic drowning arrest.
pearl: In drowning the arrest is caused by hypoxia, so ventilation comes first: five rescue breaths before chest compressions.
thinking: Pulled from water, unresponsive, gasping  ↓  Gasping is not normal breathing, so treat as cardiac arrest  ↓  Drowning causes arrest through hypoxia  ↓  Oxygenation is the priority  ↓  Open airway, five rescue breaths, then CPR
exam_trap: B tempts because she is making breathing movements, but occasional gasps are agonal and signal arrest, not adequate breathing.
takeaway: A drowning victim who is not breathing normally needs immediate resuscitation, starting with five rescue breaths.
notes: Near BX414 (man from pool, breathing inadequately, key 'secure airway and breathing'). Differentiated: child, open water, agonal gasping must be recognised as arrest, and the key is the drowning-specific sequence (five rescue breaths before compressions). Same learning point as source (start resuscitation immediately), made more specific.

stem:
A 9-year-old boy was pulled from a lake by his father after a few minutes under water. He coughed and vomited on the bank but was alert on arrival in the emergency department. Four hours later he is increasingly breathless, with crackles throughout both lung fields and falling oxygen saturations.

What is the most likely cause of his deterioration?

options.A: Spontaneous pneumothorax
options.B: Aspiration-related lung injury
options.C: Acute exacerbation of asthma
options.D: Hypothermia-induced bradycardia
options.E: Anxiety-related hyperventilation

correct_answer: B. Aspiration-related lung injury
why_correct: Water and vomit aspirated during submersion wash out surfactant and injure the alveoli, causing non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema that can appear or worsen several hours after an apparently good recovery. Bilateral crackles and falling saturations after a drowning episode fit this picture, which is why symptomatic survivors are observed in hospital. Source: Resuscitation Council UK, Special Circumstances guidelines (drowning), 2021.
why_wrong: A. A pneumothorax causes unilateral reduced breath sounds, not bilateral crackles. C. Asthma produces wheeze rather than widespread crackles, and nothing suggests he has asthma. D. Hypothermia slows the heart but does not explain bilateral crackles and hypoxia developing hours later. E. Anxiety-related hyperventilation does not cause crackles or falling oxygen saturations.
pearl: Lung injury after drowning can be delayed, so anyone with respiratory symptoms after submersion should be observed in hospital.
thinking: Submersion with coughing and vomiting  ↓  Initially alert, then breathless hours later  ↓  Bilateral crackles and hypoxia  ↓  Surfactant washout and alveolar damage  ↓  Aspiration-related lung injury
exam_trap: A might be chosen for new breathlessness, but bilateral crackles point to diffuse alveolar injury, not a pneumothorax.
takeaway: Breathlessness hours after drowning suggests aspiration-related lung injury, and symptomatic survivors need hospital observation.
notes: New vignette with delayed deterioration (child, lake, crackles, hypoxia). Distractors replaced with plausible respiratory/environmental alternatives instead of unrelated conditions (renal colic, appendicitis, migraine).

stem:
A 46-year-old woman walking on heathland in southern England is bitten on the ankle by a grey snake with a dark zig-zag stripe along its back. Within an hour her lower leg is swollen and bruised, she has vomited twice and she feels faint. A paramedic reaches her at the roadside.

What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Apply a tight tourniquet above the bite
options.B: Cut across the bite and squeeze the wound
options.C: Suck the venom out and rinse with water
options.D: Urgent hospital assessment for antivenom
options.E: Send her home to rest unless she collapses

correct_answer: D. Urgent hospital assessment for antivenom
why_correct: The adder is the only venomous snake native to the UK, and spreading swelling with vomiting and faintness indicates systemic envenoming. She needs urgent transfer to hospital with the bitten limb kept still, for monitoring and antivenom given on specialist advice (TOXBASE/National Poisons Information Service). Cutting, sucking or tight tourniquets cause harm and must not be used. Source: NHS 'Snake bites', reviewed July 2026.
why_wrong: A. A tight tourniquet risks limb ischaemia and is not recommended. B. Incising the wound adds tissue damage, bleeding and infection without removing venom. C. Sucking the wound does not remove venom and can introduce infection. E. Systemic features are already present, so delaying care until collapse is dangerous.
pearl: Vomiting, faintness or rapidly spreading swelling after an adder bite signals systemic envenoming; keep the limb still and get to hospital, where antivenom is given on specialist advice.
thinking: Grey snake with zig-zag stripe in the UK  ↓  Adder, the only venomous native snake  ↓  Spreading swelling, vomiting, faintness  ↓  Systemic envenoming  ↓  Immobilise and urgent hospital care for antivenom
exam_trap: A is a common first-aid myth; tight tourniquets cause ischaemia and are not recommended.
takeaway: Venomous snakebite with systemic features needs urgent hospital care and antivenom, never cutting, sucking or tourniquets.
notes: Re-set in a UK context (adder) for PLAB relevance; same principle (urgent medical assessment, avoid harmful first aid). Verified against NHS Snake bites page (reviewed 17 July 2026): do not cut, suck or tie anything tightly; keep limb still; antivenom in hospital.

stem:
A 24-year-old man is giving blood at a donor session. As the needle is removed he says he feels sick, turns grey and clammy, and slumps in the chair, unresponsive for a few seconds. His radial pulse is slow. Once he is laid down with his legs raised he is fully alert within a minute, with no breathlessness, lip swelling or skin changes.

Which is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Anaphylactic reaction
options.B: Hypoglycaemic episode
options.C: Generalised seizure
options.D: Cardiac arrhythmia
options.E: Vasovagal syncope

correct_answer: E. Vasovagal syncope
why_correct: A clear trigger (needle and blood donation), a prodrome of nausea, pallor and sweating, a slow pulse and complete recovery within moments of lying flat with the legs raised are typical of vasovagal (reflex) syncope. The absence of breathing difficulty, swelling or skin changes argues against anaphylaxis. Source: NICE CG109 Transient loss of consciousness ('blackouts') in over 16s, updated 2023.
why_wrong: A. Anaphylaxis causes airway, breathing or circulatory compromise, usually with skin or mucosal changes and a fast pulse, and does not settle simply on lying flat. B. Hypoglycaemia does not resolve within a minute without glucose and is not provoked by a needle. C. A seizure usually involves longer unresponsiveness, limb jerking and post-ictal confusion rather than immediate full recovery. D. An arrhythmic blackout typically occurs without a trigger or prodrome, whereas this episode follows a classic reflex pattern.
pearl: Trigger, prodrome, brief loss of consciousness and rapid full recovery when supine is the vasovagal pattern; no airway, breathing or skin features points away from anaphylaxis.
thinking: Needle and blood donation trigger  ↓  Nausea, pallor and sweating before the faint  ↓  Slow pulse during the episode  ↓  Rapid full recovery when laid flat with legs raised  ↓  Vasovagal syncope
exam_trap: A is tempting because collapse after a needle suggests a reaction, but anaphylaxis brings a fast pulse and airway, breathing or skin features.
takeaway: Collapse with a trigger, prodrome, slow pulse and rapid recovery lying flat is vasovagal syncope.
notes: New setting (blood donation rather than venepuncture on a ward); distractors changed to other causes of transient loss of consciousness. CARD059 (faint in hot room) is a different scenario.

stem:
A 58-year-old man was stung on the back of his hand by a wasp while cutting a hedge two hours ago. The skin around the sting is red, warm, itchy and swollen, and the swelling extends a short way up his wrist. He has no rash elsewhere, no lip or tongue swelling and no wheeze. His pulse, blood pressure and temperature are normal.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Local sting reaction
options.B: Anaphylactic reaction to venom
options.C: Bacterial cellulitis of the hand
options.D: Acute generalised urticaria
options.E: Hereditary angioedema attack

correct_answer: A. Local sting reaction
why_correct: Redness, swelling, warmth and itch confined to the area around a recent sting, with no features elsewhere and no airway, breathing or circulation problems, is a local reaction. It is managed with a cold compress, elevation, an oral antihistamine for itch and simple analgesia, with safety-netting about signs of infection or a systemic reaction. Source: NICE CKS Insect bites and stings, accessed 2026; NHS 'Insect bites and stings'.
why_wrong: B. Anaphylaxis requires airway, breathing or circulatory compromise, none of which is present. C. Cellulitis develops over days with spreading tenderness and often fever, not within two hours of a sting. D. Generalised urticaria would cause wheals away from the sting site, which he does not have. E. Hereditary angioedema causes recurrent non-itchy swelling without redness, not an itchy red reaction at a sting site.
pearl: Swelling and itch within hours of a sting is inflammation, not infection, so antibiotics are not needed unless signs of infection develop later.
thinking: Wasp sting two hours ago  ↓  Red, itchy, swollen area around the sting only  ↓  No airway, breathing or circulation problems and no distant rash  ↓  Too early and too itchy for cellulitis  ↓  Local sting reaction
exam_trap: C appeals because the area is red and warm, but infection takes days to develop, while inflammation within hours of a sting is expected.
takeaway: Isolated red, itchy swelling around a recent sting with normal observations is a local reaction.
notes: New vignette; cellulitis and hereditary angioedema added as more discriminating distractors in place of septic shock and meningitis.

stem:
A 71-year-old widower has had dull headaches, nausea and tiredness for three weeks, since the weather turned cold. They ease when he spends the day at his daughter's house. Blood tests show a raised carboxyhaemoglobin level, and a home safety visit is arranged.

Which household item is the most likely source of his exposure?

options.A: Electric storage heater in the hall
options.B: Gas boiler with a blocked flue
options.C: Microwave oven used for every meal
options.D: Induction hob used for cooking
options.E: Oil-filled electric radiator

correct_answer: B. Gas boiler with a blocked flue
why_correct: Carbon monoxide is produced by incomplete burning of carbon-based fuels, so faulty, poorly maintained or poorly ventilated combustion appliances such as gas boilers are the classic household source. Electrical appliances burn no fuel and cannot produce it. Source: NHS 'Carbon monoxide poisoning', accessed 2026; UKHSA Carbon monoxide: incident management and toxicology.
why_wrong: A. A storage heater warms electrically and burns no fuel, so it cannot generate carbon monoxide. C. A microwave heats food electrically and produces no combustion gases. D. An induction hob uses electromagnetic heating with no flame or fuel. E. An oil-filled radiator is sealed and electrically heated, so it does not produce carbon monoxide.
pearl: Carbon monoxide comes from burning fuel, so ask about gas, oil, coal or wood appliances, barbecues or engines in enclosed spaces, and advise an audible carbon monoxide alarm.
thinking: Headache, nausea and tiredness since the heating season began  ↓  Better away from home, raised carboxyhaemoglobin  ↓  Carbon monoxide comes from incomplete combustion  ↓  Look for a fuel-burning appliance  ↓  Gas boiler with a blocked flue
exam_trap: A or E may appeal because symptoms began with the cold weather, but only appliances that burn fuel produce carbon monoxide.
takeaway: Household carbon monoxide comes from faulty or poorly ventilated fuel-burning appliances.
notes: Source was a bare recall item; built a clinical vignette around the same fact. Distractors made plausible (all heating/cooking appliances, all electric) instead of tap water/food. BX688 tests the diagnosis, not the source, so not a duplicate.

stem:
An 83-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease was started on regular oral morphine for back pain five days ago. Her carer finds her very difficult to rouse. Her breathing is slow and shallow and both pupils are pinpoint. She is not sweating or drooling, and her capillary blood glucose is normal.

Which is the most likely cause of her presentation?

options.A: Benzodiazepine toxicity
options.B: Organophosphate poisoning
options.C: Hypoglycaemic coma
options.D: Opioid toxicity
options.E: Carbon monoxide poisoning

correct_answer: D. Opioid toxicity
why_correct: Reduced consciousness, slow breathing and pinpoint pupils make up the opioid toxidrome. Morphine and its active metabolites are cleared by the kidneys, so they accumulate in chronic kidney disease even at standard doses; she needs airway support and titrated naloxone, with the morphine stopped. Source: BNF, Morphine (renal impairment), accessed 2026; TOXBASE opioids.
why_wrong: A. Benzodiazepine toxicity causes drowsiness but does not typically produce pinpoint pupils. B. Organophosphate poisoning also causes small pupils but brings sweating, salivation and bronchorrhoea, which are absent. C. A normal capillary glucose excludes hypoglycaemia. E. Carbon monoxide poisoning causes headache and confusion without pinpoint pupils or marked respiratory slowing.
pearl: Opioids accumulate in renal impairment, so in kidney disease use lower doses, longer intervals or a safer alternative, and watch for drowsiness and slow breathing.
thinking: Elderly, chronic kidney disease, recently started morphine  ↓  Hard to rouse with slow breathing  ↓  Pinpoint pupils without cholinergic features  ↓  Renal accumulation of morphine and metabolites  ↓  Opioid toxicity
exam_trap: B is tempting because organophosphates also cause small pupils, but the absence of sweating, salivation and bronchorrhoea points to opioids.
takeaway: Drowsiness, slow breathing and pinpoint pupils mean opioid toxicity, which can arise from accumulation in kidney disease.
notes: Near BX386 (young man, unknown amount of opioid) and ACU016 cover deliberate/illicit overdose; this version uses a different scenario (iatrogenic accumulation in CKD) leading to the same diagnosis. Respiratory rate figure softened to words.

stem:
A 20-year-old student attends the emergency department five hours after swallowing a large number of paracetamol tablets following an argument. She says she feels completely fine, is eating a sandwich, and wants to leave because she believes the tablets 'have not done anything'.

Which statement best explains why her lack of symptoms is not reassuring?

options.A: Paracetamol is only harmful if taken with alcohol
options.B: Its effects are hidden by its own pain-relieving action
options.C: Tablets stay in the stomach for days before absorption
options.D: Its main toxicity is to the kidneys, not the liver
options.E: Liver injury develops silently over the next few days

correct_answer: E. Liver injury develops silently over the next few days
why_correct: A toxic metabolite of paracetamol depletes liver glutathione and damages hepatocytes, but symptoms such as right upper quadrant pain, vomiting and jaundice usually appear only a day or more later. Early on, patients often feel well despite a potentially fatal ingestion, so risk is judged on the timing, amount and a timed plasma paracetamol level, alongside a psychosocial assessment. Source: MHRA Drug Safety Update, Treating paracetamol overdose with intravenous acetylcysteine, 2012; NICE NG225 Self-harm, 2022.
why_wrong: A. Paracetamol alone can cause fatal liver failure; alcohol is not required for toxicity. B. Paracetamol's analgesic effect does not mask liver injury; the damage simply has not yet produced symptoms. C. Paracetamol is absorbed rapidly from the gut, so delayed absorption does not explain her lack of symptoms. D. The liver is the main target organ; kidney injury can occur but is secondary.
pearl: Feeling well after a paracetamol overdose is expected early and is never reassuring; treatment decisions rest on timing and blood levels.
thinking: Large paracetamol overdose five hours ago  ↓  Patient feels well and wants to leave  ↓  Toxic metabolite injures liver cells silently  ↓  Symptoms appear a day or more later  ↓  Absence of symptoms is not reassuring
exam_trap: B sounds plausible, but analgesia does not hide liver damage; the injury is simply silent at first.
takeaway: Paracetamol liver injury is silent early, so a well-looking patient still needs full assessment.
notes: New vignette (patient wanting to leave). Note for reviewer: capacity and self-harm risk assessment would also be needed if she tried to leave; mentioned via NG225 in why_correct. BX387/NEP031 test next steps, not the reason for early silence.

stem:
A 52-year-old man is brought in by his wife after he took a whole box of her prescribed diazepam about three hours ago. He is drowsy but rousable to voice, protecting his own airway and breathing comfortably. His heart rate, blood pressure and oxygen saturations are normal. Paracetamol and salicylate are undetectable, and no other substances are suspected.

What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Supportive care with close observation
options.B: Intravenous flumazenil to reverse sedation
options.C: Urgent haemodialysis to remove the drug
options.D: Gastric lavage via an orogastric tube
options.E: Intravenous naloxone as a precaution

correct_answer: A. Supportive care with close observation
why_correct: Isolated benzodiazepine overdose usually causes drowsiness with preserved breathing and circulation and is rarely life-threatening on its own. Management is supportive: monitor airway, breathing, consciousness and observations until he wakes, then arrange a psychosocial assessment. Source: TOXBASE (NPIS) benzodiazepines, accessed 2026; NICE NG225 Self-harm, 2022.
why_wrong: B. Flumazenil is not used routinely in overdose because it can precipitate seizures, particularly with benzodiazepine dependence or mixed ingestions. C. Benzodiazepines are highly protein-bound and are not effectively removed by dialysis. D. Gastric lavage is not recommended in benzodiazepine overdose and risks aspiration in a drowsy patient. E. Naloxone reverses opioids and has no role when no opioid has been taken.
pearl: Most benzodiazepine overdoses settle with supportive care; flumazenil is a specialist decision, not routine reversal.
thinking: Large diazepam ingestion  ↓  Drowsy but rousable, airway protected  ↓  Stable observations, no co-ingestants  ↓  Rarely dangerous alone, and the antidote carries seizure risk  ↓  Supportive care and observation
exam_trap: B appeals because flumazenil is the benzodiazepine antagonist, but in overdose it can provoke seizures and is not given routinely.
takeaway: Isolated benzodiazepine overdose with stable observations is managed supportively.
notes: New vignette; distractors now include flumazenil, lavage and naloxone (more discriminating than warfarin reversal/insulin). REVIEWER FLAG: existing live item BX275 (deeply drowsy, hypoventilating diazepam overdose) is keyed 'Flumazenil'; worth checking it is consistent with TOXBASE advice that flumazenil is not routine in overdose.

stem:
A 38-year-old recreational diver off the Cornish coast ran low on air and surfaced quickly from a deep dive, missing her safety stop. Forty minutes later she has a deep ache in both shoulders, tingling and weakness in her legs, and an itchy mottled rash over her chest.

Which is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Nitrogen narcosis
options.B: Decompression sickness
options.C: Rotator cuff strain
options.D: Hypoglycaemia
options.E: Exertional rhabdomyolysis

correct_answer: B. Decompression sickness
why_correct: Ascending too fast lets nitrogen dissolved in the tissues come out of solution as bubbles, causing joint pain ('the bends'), neurological symptoms and skin mottling within minutes to hours of surfacing. Treatment is 100% oxygen, lying flat, fluids and urgent discussion with a diving medicine service for hyperbaric recompression. Source: British Hyperbaric Association / UK Diving Medical Committee guidance, accessed 2026.
why_wrong: A. Nitrogen narcosis impairs judgement at depth and resolves on ascent rather than starting after surfacing. C. A rotator cuff strain would not cause bilateral shoulder pain with leg weakness and a rash. D. Hypoglycaemia does not explain joint pain, neurological signs and skin mottling after a rapid ascent. E. Rhabdomyolysis causes muscle pain and dark urine after crush injury or extreme exertion, not joint pain with neurological signs after diving.
pearl: Any new symptom after diving is decompression illness until proven otherwise; give 100% oxygen and contact a recompression service urgently.
thinking: Rapid ascent with a missed safety stop  ↓  Symptoms within an hour of surfacing  ↓  Joint pain, neurological signs, mottled skin  ↓  Nitrogen bubbles in tissues and blood  ↓  Decompression sickness
exam_trap: A is tempting as another diving illness, but narcosis occurs at depth and clears on ascent.
takeaway: Joint pain and neurological symptoms after a rapid dive ascent mean decompression sickness, needing oxygen and recompression.
notes: New vignette with skin signs; nitrogen narcosis added as a diving-specific distractor. Depth/time figures omitted.

stem:
A 29-year-old man trekking in Nepal reached a high-altitude lodge yesterday after a fast ascent. Since last night he has had a worsening headache and vomiting. This morning his companions find him drowsy and muddled, and he cannot walk heel-to-toe in a straight line. He has no cough and is not breathless at rest.

Which is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Acute mountain sickness
options.B: High-altitude pulmonary oedema
options.C: High-altitude cerebral oedema
options.D: Exercise-associated hyponatraemia
options.E: Migraine with brainstem aura

correct_answer: C. High-altitude cerebral oedema
why_correct: Headache and vomiting at altitude are acute mountain sickness, but the addition of confusion, drowsiness and ataxia marks progression to high-altitude cerebral oedema, a life-threatening emergency. Immediate descent is the priority, with oxygen and dexamethasone as adjuncts. Source: Wilderness Medical Society clinical practice guidelines for acute altitude illness, 2024 update.
why_wrong: A. Acute mountain sickness causes headache, nausea and fatigue, but confusion and ataxia mean it has progressed to cerebral oedema. B. High-altitude pulmonary oedema causes breathlessness at rest, cough and reduced exercise tolerance, which he does not have. D. Hyponatraemia can cause confusion, but headache, vomiting and ataxia after a rapid ascent fit altitude illness far better. E. Migraine should not be assumed at altitude when drowsiness and ataxia are present.
pearl: Ataxia or altered consciousness at altitude is high-altitude cerebral oedema until proven otherwise; descend immediately.
thinking: Rapid ascent to high altitude  ↓  Headache and vomiting suggest acute mountain sickness  ↓  New drowsiness, confusion and ataxia  ↓  Progression to cerebral oedema  ↓  HACE: descend, oxygen, dexamethasone
exam_trap: A is the trap: headache and vomiting fit acute mountain sickness, but ataxia and confusion define cerebral oedema.
takeaway: At altitude, confusion or ataxia means high-altitude cerebral oedema, which needs immediate descent.
notes: Kept Difficult by adding acute mountain sickness and hyponatraemia as close distractors (replacing gastroenteritis/heat exhaustion). Altitude figure omitted.

stem:
A 41-year-old man was standing beside a gas barbecue when the canister exploded. He has superficial burns to his face and neck, singed eyebrows and nasal hairs, and his voice has become slightly hoarse over the past hour. He is talking, has no stridor and his oxygen saturations are normal. The emergency physician asks a senior anaesthetist to assess him now.

What is the main reason for this early airway assessment?

options.A: Hoarseness after burns usually reflects anxiety
options.B: Tension pneumothorax commonly follows blast burns
options.C: Airway swelling is at its worst at the moment of injury
options.D: He needs early oral fluids to prevent dehydration
options.E: Airway oedema can worsen and make intubation hard

correct_answer: E. Airway oedema can worsen and make intubation hard
why_correct: Facial burns, singed nasal hair and new hoarseness suggest thermal injury to the upper airway. Oedema develops over the following hours, especially once fluid resuscitation starts, so an airway that is patent now may become impossible to intubate later; early senior anaesthetic assessment allows planned intubation before obstruction. Source: ATLS, American College of Surgeons (current edition); British Burn Association guidance, accessed 2026.
why_wrong: A. Hoarseness after facial burns is a warning sign of airway injury and must not be put down to anxiety. B. Tension pneumothorax is not the expected threat here; the concern is upper airway swelling. C. Airway oedema after burns increases over the following hours rather than being maximal at the time of injury. D. Oral intake is not a priority and may be unsafe before the airway has been secured.
pearl: Normal saturations and no stridor do not exclude airway burns; hoarseness after facial burns is the cue to secure the airway early.
thinking: Flash burn to face and neck  ↓  Singed nasal hair and new hoarseness  ↓  Thermal upper airway injury  ↓  Oedema worsens over hours, especially with fluids  ↓  Early senior airway assessment before obstruction
exam_trap: C is tempting, but burn-related airway swelling builds over hours, so waiting for stridor is too late.
takeaway: Suspected airway burns need early senior airway assessment because oedema progresses and makes later intubation difficult.
notes: Near ACU034 (house fire, stridor already present). Differentiated: flash burn without stridor, normal saturations, asking why to act before signs of obstruction.

stem:
A 33-year-old railway engineer touched a high-voltage overhead cable. He has a small charred wound on his right palm and another on the sole of his right foot, with little visible skin damage in between. His right forearm is becoming tense and painful, and his urine is dark.

Why is his injury likely to be far worse than the skin wounds suggest?

options.A: Current travels through deep tissues along its path
options.B: High-voltage injuries damage only the surface layers of skin
options.C: Dark urine is caused by the burn dressings
options.D: Muscle is resistant to electrical damage
options.E: The size of the skin wound reliably reflects the depth of injury

correct_answer: A. Current travels through deep tissues along its path
why_correct: Electrical current travels between entry and exit points through muscle, nerves and blood vessels, generating heat and cell damage deep beneath relatively normal-looking skin. Here a tense forearm and dark urine suggest muscle necrosis with compartment syndrome and rhabdomyolysis, so he needs an ECG, creatine kinase, renal monitoring and urgent surgical review. Source: British Burn Association guidance; NICE CKS Burns and scalds, accessed 2026.
why_wrong: B. High-voltage current commonly causes extensive deep tissue destruction beneath small skin wounds. C. Dark urine here reflects myoglobin from damaged muscle, not the dressings. D. Muscle is particularly vulnerable to electrical injury, and its breakdown causes rhabdomyolysis. E. Skin wounds greatly underestimate the extent of internal electrical injury.
pearl: In electrical injury the skin wound is the tip of the iceberg; check an ECG, creatine kinase and urine, and watch for compartment syndrome.
thinking: High-voltage contact with entry and exit wounds  ↓  Current passes through the limb between them  ↓  Deep muscle and nerve damage under small skin wounds  ↓  Tense forearm and dark urine  ↓  Deep injury far exceeds the visible burn
exam_trap: E appeals to ordinary burns logic, but in electrical injury small skin wounds can hide massive deep damage.
takeaway: Electrical burns are judged by the current's path through deep tissue, not by the size of the skin wound.
notes: BX413 tests arrhythmia risk after a minor shock; this tests the mechanism of deep injury with a high-voltage entry/exit scenario, so not a duplicate.

stem:
A 16-year-old boy has felt feverish and achy since last night, which his parents put down to flu. This afternoon he complains of severe pains in his legs, and although he feels hot his hands and feet are cold and he looks unusually pale. He is alert, with no headache, neck stiffness or dislike of bright light. When he is undressed, three small purple spots on his abdomen do not fade when a glass is pressed on them.

Which is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Influenza with viral myalgia
options.B: Meningococcal septicaemia
options.C: IgA vasculitis (Henoch–Schönlein purpura)
options.D: Immune thrombocytopenia
options.E: Infectious mononucleosis

correct_answer: B. Meningococcal septicaemia
why_correct: Leg pain, cold hands and feet and pallor in a feverish young person are early signs of sepsis that often appear before the rash spreads, and any non-blanching spots with fever indicate meningococcal septicaemia until proven otherwise. Headache and neck stiffness are frequently absent when septicaemia occurs without meningitis, so their absence must not reassure; he needs immediate antibiotics (benzylpenicillin in primary care if it does not delay transfer, ceftriaxone in hospital) and emergency hospital care. Source: NICE NG240 Meningitis (bacterial) and meningococcal disease, 2024.
why_wrong: A. Influenza causes fever and aching but not non-blanching spots or cold peripheries with pallor. C. IgA vasculitis gives palpable purpura over the legs and buttocks, often with joint and abdominal pain, in a child who is not septic. D. Immune thrombocytopenia causes petechiae and bruising in a child who is usually afebrile and otherwise well. E. Infectious mononucleosis causes fever with sore throat, swollen lymph nodes and tiredness, not leg pain, cold peripheries and non-blanching spots on the trunk.
pearl: Leg pain, cold hands and feet and pallor are early warning signs of meningococcal septicaemia that can appear before meningism or a widespread rash.
thinking: Feverish teenager thought to have flu  ↓  Severe leg pain, cold hands and feet, pallor  ↓  Early signs of sepsis  ↓  A few non-blanching spots, no meningism  ↓  Meningococcal septicaemia
exam_trap: A is tempting because the illness began like flu, but cold peripheries, leg pain and any non-blanching spot point to meningococcal septicaemia.
takeaway: A feverish young person with any non-blanching spots has meningococcal septicaemia until proven otherwise, even without neck stiffness.
notes: Source scenario (teenager, fever, meningism, non-blanching rash) duplicates live BX420/NEU036/ID014/ACU024, so re-angled to a toddler with septicaemia and NO meningism: same diagnosis, different scenario (rule 3). Chickenpox/migraine distractors replaced with paediatric rash mimics.

stem:
A 45-year-old man telephones his GP surgery and tells the duty doctor he swallowed a large number of paracetamol tablets about three hours ago because he 'could not cope'. He feels fine, has no abdominal pain, and asks whether he can just stay at home and see how he goes.

What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Advise him to attend if abdominal pain or jaundice develops
options.B: Arrange liver function tests at the surgery tomorrow
options.C: Arrange immediate emergency department assessment
options.D: Advise him to make himself vomit, then rest at home
options.E: Book a routine mental health review for next week

correct_answer: C. Arrange immediate emergency department assessment
why_correct: After a deliberate paracetamol overdose patients often feel well for the first day despite potentially fatal liver injury, so he needs same-day emergency department assessment: establish timing and dose, take a timed paracetamol level, start acetylcysteine as indicated and carry out a psychosocial assessment of his self-harm. Emergency transport should be arranged if there is any doubt that he will attend safely. Source: NICE NG225 Self-harm, 2022; MHRA Drug Safety Update on paracetamol overdose, 2012.
why_wrong: A. Waiting for symptoms is unsafe because liver failure appears late, when acetylcysteine is less effective. B. Delaying blood tests until tomorrow misses the period in which acetylcysteine works best. D. Inducing vomiting is not recommended and does not prevent paracetamol toxicity. E. A routine review ignores both the urgent physical danger and the immediate self-harm risk.
pearl: Any deliberate paracetamol overdose needs same-day hospital assessment, however well the patient feels, plus a psychosocial assessment.
thinking: Deliberate paracetamol overdose three hours ago  ↓  Feels well, but early toxicity is silent  ↓  Treatment depends on timing and a timed level  ↓  Self-harm risk also needs assessment  ↓  Immediate emergency department assessment
exam_trap: A sounds pragmatic, but symptoms of liver damage appear too late for the antidote to work well.
takeaway: Deliberate paracetamol overdose always needs urgent hospital assessment, regardless of symptoms.
notes: Re-angled to a primary-care telephone scenario to avoid duplicating BX387 (ED patient several hours after intentional overdose, key 'establish timing, bloods and treatment'). Same learning point: do not wait for symptoms; urgent paracetamol-poisoning pathway plus self-harm assessment.

stem:
A mother brings her 2-year-old daughter, who has had none of her routine vaccinations, to the GP surgery because over the past four hours she has developed a high fever and become quiet and unwell. The child is sitting upright on her mother's knee with her chin pushed forward, saliva running from her mouth and a soft stridor. She will not speak and looks pale and frightened.

What is the most appropriate immediate action by the GP?

options.A: Examine her throat with a tongue depressor to confirm it
options.B: Give oral dexamethasone and review her in one hour
options.C: Lie her flat on the couch and give oxygen by mask
options.D: Call 999 and keep her calm and upright with her mother
options.E: Ask her mother to drive her straight to the emergency department

correct_answer: D. Call 999 and keep her calm and upright with her mother
why_correct: A rapid high fever with drooling, stridor, refusal to speak and an upright, chin-forward posture in an unvaccinated child suggests acute epiglottitis, which can obstruct the airway suddenly. In primary care she should be kept calm and upright with her parent, without examining the throat or lying her down, and transferred by emergency ambulance with a pre-alert so that senior anaesthetic and ENT staff can secure the airway. Source: NHS 'Epiglottitis', accessed 2026; Advanced Paediatric Life Support (ALSG).
why_wrong: A. Examining the throat can provoke laryngospasm and complete airway obstruction. B. Dexamethasone and review is croup management and delays emergency care for a threatened airway. C. Lying her flat and forcing a mask on her may distress her and worsen obstruction; she should stay in the upright position she has chosen. E. Travelling by car leaves no one able to manage her airway if it obstructs on the way.
pearl: In suspected epiglottitis outside hospital, leave the child upright with a parent, do not look in the throat, and send by 999 ambulance with a pre-alert.
thinking: Unvaccinated toddler with high fever over hours  ↓  Drooling, stridor, refusing to speak, sitting chin-forward  ↓  Acute epiglottitis  ↓  Distress or examination may cause complete obstruction  ↓  Keep calm and upright, 999 transfer
exam_trap: B is tempting because stridor in a toddler suggests croup, but drooling, toxicity and rapid onset point to epiglottitis, which needs emergency transfer.
takeaway: A child with suspected epiglottitis in primary care needs a 999 ambulance, kept calm and upright, with no throat examination.
notes: New vignette (unimmunised, Hib risk). Distractors upgraded (cannulation, X-ray, croup treatment) from food/discharge. BX944 asks the diagnosis; this asks management, so not a duplicate.

stem:
A 30-year-old woman arrives six hours after taking a single handful of paracetamol tablets at a known time, following a row with her partner. She is alert and has no symptoms. Blood is taken for several tests.

Which result is the main guide to whether she needs acetylcysteine?

options.A: Plasma paracetamol concentration
options.B: Venous blood gas pH and lactate level
options.C: Serum alanine aminotransferase
options.D: International normalised ratio
options.E: Serum creatinine and urea

correct_answer: A. Plasma paracetamol concentration
why_correct: For a single ingestion at a known time, a plasma paracetamol concentration taken at least 4 hours after ingestion is plotted against time on the treatment nomogram; a level on or above the treatment line means acetylcysteine is needed. Liver tests and INR are taken at the same time, but early on they are often normal and do not predict risk. Source: MHRA Drug Safety Update, Treating paracetamol overdose with intravenous acetylcysteine, 2012; TOXBASE.
why_wrong: B. Blood gas and lactate help in severe or late poisoning but do not stratify risk in a well patient early after ingestion. C. ALT is often normal in the first hours, so a normal result does not exclude a toxic ingestion. D. INR rises only once liver injury is established and is used for monitoring rather than for the initial treatment decision. E. Renal function is monitored but does not determine the need for the antidote.
pearl: A level taken less than 4 hours after a single ingestion cannot be interpreted; at 4 hours or later, plot it against time to decide on acetylcysteine.
thinking: Single paracetamol overdose at a known time  ↓  Six hours since ingestion, so a level can be interpreted  ↓  Early liver tests may still be normal  ↓  Plot the plasma level against time on the nomogram  ↓  Paracetamol concentration decides treatment
exam_trap: C appeals because paracetamol damages the liver, but ALT is often normal early and does not exclude a toxic dose.
takeaway: After a timed single paracetamol overdose, the plasma level plotted against time decides on acetylcysteine.
notes: Re-angled from 'next step' to 'which result decides treatment' (ALT/INR as close distractors) to separate it from NEP031 (when to take the level) and BX387. Kept the 4-hour figure as a PLAB-relied fact in explanations only; the key does not hinge on recalling a movable threshold.

stem:
A 67-year-old woman of low body weight has been taking extra paracetamol for severe toothache over the past four days, together with an over-the-counter cold remedy that also contains paracetamol. She now feels nauseated and has right upper quadrant tenderness. Her ALT is markedly raised.

Which treatment should be started to limit further liver injury?

options.A: Intravenous naloxone infusion
options.B: Intravenous acetylcysteine
options.C: Oral activated charcoal suspension
options.D: Intravenous vitamin K (phytomenadione)
options.E: Intravenous fomepizole

correct_answer: B. Intravenous acetylcysteine
why_correct: Repeated supratherapeutic or staggered paracetamol intake can cause liver injury, particularly in people of low body weight, and the treatment nomogram cannot be used because there is no single ingestion time. With symptoms and a raised ALT she should start intravenous acetylcysteine without delay; it replenishes glutathione, which detoxifies the toxic metabolite NAPQI. Source: MHRA Drug Safety Update, 2012; TOXBASE paracetamol guidance.
why_wrong: A. Naloxone reverses opioid toxicity and has no effect on paracetamol liver injury. C. Activated charcoal is useful only within about an hour of ingestion and has no role after days of intake. D. Vitamin K may correct a raised INR but does not protect the liver from ongoing paracetamol toxicity. E. Fomepizole blocks alcohol dehydrogenase and is used for methanol or ethylene glycol poisoning.
pearl: In staggered or repeated excess paracetamol intake the nomogram does not apply; start acetylcysteine and seek TOXBASE or poisons service advice.
thinking: Several days of excess paracetamol from two products  ↓  Low body weight increases risk  ↓  Nausea, right upper quadrant tenderness, raised ALT  ↓  No single ingestion time, so the nomogram cannot be used  ↓  Start intravenous acetylcysteine
exam_trap: D is tempting if a raised INR is expected, but vitamin K does not treat the cause; acetylcysteine is the antidote.
takeaway: Acetylcysteine is the antidote for paracetamol toxicity, including staggered and therapeutic-excess ingestions.
notes: Source was a bare recall item; built a vignette. Acute single-overdose 'level above line -> NAC' scenarios already live (GAS012, CP010, ACU019), so used a therapeutic-excess/staggered scenario to avoid duplication; same learning point (acetylcysteine is the antidote). Weight threshold deliberately not stated (rule 2).

presentation: Accidental opioid ingestion in a child
stem:
A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after his grandmother found him with her opened bottle of methadone oral solution about an hour ago. He is now very drowsy, his breathing is slow and shallow, and his pupils are pinpoint. His oxygen saturations remain low despite bag-valve-mask ventilation with oxygen.

Which drug should be given to reverse his condition?

options.A: Flumazenil
options.B: Atropine
options.C: Glucagon
options.D: Naloxone
options.E: Acetylcysteine

correct_answer: D. Naloxone
why_correct: Drowsiness, slow shallow breathing and pinpoint pupils after access to methadone indicate opioid toxicity, which is reversed by the opioid antagonist naloxone given while breathing is supported. Methadone acts for much longer than naloxone, so toxicity often returns as naloxone wears off; repeat doses or an infusion, prolonged observation in hospital and advice from TOXBASE or the National Poisons Information Service are needed, and the circumstances should be explored as a safeguarding matter. Source: BNF for Children, Naloxone hydrochloride, accessed 2026; TOXBASE methadone.
why_wrong: A. Flumazenil antagonises benzodiazepines, not opioids. B. Atropine treats bradycardia or muscarinic toxicity and does not reverse opioid effects. C. Glucagon is used for hypoglycaemia and beta-blocker toxicity, not opioid poisoning. E. Acetylcysteine is the antidote for paracetamol poisoning.
pearl: Naloxone wears off sooner than long-acting opioids such as methadone, so expect recurrence and observe for longer, with repeat doses or an infusion if needed.
thinking: Toddler with access to methadone  ↓  Drowsy, slow shallow breathing, pinpoint pupils  ↓  Opioid toxicity  ↓  Support breathing and reverse with an opioid antagonist  ↓  Naloxone, watching for recurrence
exam_trap: A is the trap: flumazenil is also a reversal agent, but for benzodiazepines, not opioids.
takeaway: Opioid toxicity, including accidental methadone ingestion in a child, is reversed with naloxone, with prolonged monitoring for recurrence.
notes: Source was a bare recall item. Live CP031/ACU016/BX274 already cover the illicit/collapsed overdose scenario with naloxone, so used a post-operative PCA scenario (same learning point, different setting; adds titration teaching). Fomepizole distractor replaced by glucagon.

stem:
A 35-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by a friend, who found an empty strip of his prescribed diazepam tablets beside him an hour ago. No alcohol or other drugs are thought to be involved.

Which combination of findings is he most likely to show?

options.A: Agitation, dilated pupils, tachycardia and hyperthermia
options.B: Hot dry skin, dilated pupils and urinary retention
options.C: Sweating, salivation, small pupils and diarrhoea
options.D: Rapid deep breathing, tinnitus and vomiting
options.E: Drowsiness, slurred speech and unsteady gait

correct_answer: E. Drowsiness, slurred speech and unsteady gait
why_correct: Benzodiazepines enhance GABA-mediated inhibition, so overdose produces central nervous system depression: drowsiness, slurred speech, ataxia and nystagmus, usually with preserved breathing and stable observations. Severe respiratory depression is uncommon unless alcohol, opioids or other sedatives have also been taken. Source: TOXBASE (NPIS) benzodiazepines, accessed 2026.
why_wrong: A. Agitation, dilated pupils, tachycardia and hyperthermia describe a sympathomimetic picture, as with cocaine or amphetamines. B. Hot dry skin, dilated pupils and urinary retention suggest anticholinergic toxicity, for example from tricyclic antidepressants or antihistamines. C. Sweating, salivation, small pupils and diarrhoea are cholinergic features, as in organophosphate poisoning. D. Rapid deep breathing, tinnitus and vomiting point to salicylate poisoning.
pearl: Isolated benzodiazepine overdose looks like drunkenness without alcohol: sleepy, slurred and unsteady, with breathing usually preserved.
thinking: Diazepam overdose alone  ↓  Enhanced GABA inhibition  ↓  Central nervous system depression  ↓  Breathing and circulation usually preserved  ↓  Drowsiness, slurred speech, ataxia
exam_trap: C may tempt because of the small pupils, but the 'wet' cholinergic features belong to organophosphates, not benzodiazepines.
takeaway: Benzodiazepine overdose causes CNS depression with drowsiness, slurred speech and ataxia.
notes: Re-angled from a one-word feature ('CNS depression', given away by the stem's 'excessively drowsy') to toxidrome recognition with clinical-finding clusters; same learning point.

stem:
A 74-year-old man is having a diagnostic colonoscopy under intravenous midazolam sedation. Towards the end of the procedure he becomes unrousable and his breathing slows, and his oxygen saturations fall despite airway support and supplemental oxygen. He has received no opioid and has no history of seizures or long-term benzodiazepine use.

Which drug is the specific antagonist for this sedative?

options.A: Flumazenil
options.B: Naloxone
options.C: Protamine sulfate
options.D: Atropine
options.E: Glycopyrronium

correct_answer: A. Flumazenil
why_correct: Midazolam is a benzodiazepine, and flumazenil is a competitive benzodiazepine receptor antagonist used to reverse benzodiazepine sedation after procedures. It acts within minutes but is shorter-acting than many benzodiazepines, so re-sedation can occur and monitoring must continue. Source: BNF, Flumazenil, accessed 2026; Academy of Medical Royal Colleges, Safe sedation practice for healthcare procedures: an update, 2021.
why_wrong: B. Naloxone reverses opioids, and no opioid has been given here. C. Protamine reverses heparin and has no effect on sedation. D. Atropine treats bradycardia and muscarinic effects but does not reverse benzodiazepines. E. Glycopyrronium is an antimuscarinic used to reduce secretions or treat bradycardia, not to reverse sedation.
pearl: Flumazenil is used mainly to reverse procedural benzodiazepine sedation; in overdose it is avoided routinely because it can precipitate seizures, especially in dependence or mixed ingestions.
thinking: Midazolam sedation for colonoscopy  ↓  Oversedation with falling saturations despite support  ↓  No opioid given, no seizure or dependence risk  ↓  Benzodiazepine effect needs reversal  ↓  Flumazenil
exam_trap: B is the reflex choice for any oversedated patient, but naloxone only reverses opioids.
takeaway: Flumazenil is the benzodiazepine antagonist, used chiefly to reverse procedural sedation.
notes: Source was a bare recall item ('severe benzodiazepine toxicity'). Set in procedural sedation, which is flumazenil's main licensed use, and stated no seizure/dependence risk so the key is safe; this also avoids duplicating BX275 (diazepam overdose keyed flumazenil).

stem:
A 34-year-old man has had headaches and nausea most mornings since moving into an older rented flat in November. He feels better during his working day and was well on a weekend away. His cat has become unusually sleepy. His pulse oximetry reading is normal.

Which exposure is most likely to explain his symptoms?

options.A: Radon gas
options.B: Carbon monoxide
options.C: Household mould spores
options.D: Lead from old paintwork
options.E: Methane from a gas leak

correct_answer: B. Carbon monoxide
why_correct: Headache and nausea that are worse at home and ease elsewhere, with a pet also affected, are classic clues to carbon monoxide poisoning from a faulty fuel-burning appliance. Standard pulse oximetry cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin, so a normal reading does not exclude it; the diagnosis is confirmed with carboxyhaemoglobin on a blood gas. Source: NHS 'Carbon monoxide poisoning', accessed 2026; UKHSA Carbon monoxide: incident management and toxicology.
why_wrong: A. Radon causes no acute symptoms; its harm is a long-term increase in lung cancer risk. C. Mould can worsen asthma or rhinitis but does not cause daily headaches that clear on leaving home or make pets drowsy. D. Lead poisoning develops over months with abdominal pain, anaemia and neuropathy rather than symptoms that clear on leaving home. E. Natural gas (methane) is not itself toxic; its dangers are fire, explosion or asphyxia, and mains gas carries an added smell.
pearl: Symptoms that improve away from home, other people or pets affected, and a normal pulse oximetry reading are classic clues to carbon monoxide.
thinking: Morning headache and nausea at home  ↓  Better at work and away  ↓  Pet also affected  ↓  Normal pulse oximetry does not exclude it  ↓  Carbon monoxide
exam_trap: A normal pulse oximetry reading may seem to exclude a toxic gas, but standard oximeters read carboxyhaemoglobin as oxygenated haemoglobin.
takeaway: Symptoms that improve away from home suggest carbon monoxide, even with normal pulse oximetry.
notes: Source scenario (several household members, winter, better away) duplicates live BX688 (diagnosis) closely, so re-angled to a single occupant with a sleepy pet and normal oximetry: different scenario, same diagnosis (rule 3). Distractors now household exposures.

stem:
Two friends camping in a small tent in the Lake District light a charcoal barbecue inside it to keep warm. The next morning one of them, a 27-year-old woman, is brought to hospital with headache, vomiting and confusion. Her skin colour is normal and her pulse oximetry reading is normal on air.

Which test will confirm the suspected diagnosis?

options.A: Methaemoglobin on co-oximetry
options.B: Repeat pulse oximetry on another finger
options.C: Carboxyhaemoglobin on a blood gas
options.D: Serum troponin concentration
options.E: Serum lactate concentration

correct_answer: C. Carboxyhaemoglobin on a blood gas
why_correct: Burning charcoal in an enclosed space produces carbon monoxide, which binds haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin. Standard pulse oximeters read carboxyhaemoglobin as oxygenated haemoglobin and give falsely reassuring values, so the diagnosis is confirmed by measuring carboxyhaemoglobin on an arterial or venous blood gas with co-oximetry; high-flow oxygen should not wait for the result. Source: NHS 'Carbon monoxide poisoning', accessed 2026; TOXBASE carbon monoxide.
why_wrong: A. Methaemoglobin rises with oxidising agents such as nitrites or dapsone, not carbon monoxide. B. Repeating standard pulse oximetry will give the same falsely normal reading. D. Troponin may be checked for myocardial injury but does not diagnose carbon monoxide exposure. E. Lactate may be raised in severe poisoning but is non-specific.
pearl: Carbon monoxide fools the pulse oximeter, so measure carboxyhaemoglobin on a co-oximetry blood gas and give high-flow oxygen meanwhile.
thinking: Charcoal burned in an enclosed tent  ↓  Headache, vomiting, confusion  ↓  Pulse oximetry falsely normal  ↓  Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin as carboxyhaemoglobin  ↓  Measure carboxyhaemoglobin on a blood gas
exam_trap: B appeals if the normal oximetry seems wrong, but any standard oximeter misreads carboxyhaemoglobin as oxyhaemoglobin.
takeaway: Confirm suspected carbon monoxide poisoning with carboxyhaemoglobin on a co-oximetry blood gas.
notes: New scenario (charcoal in a tent). Added falsely normal pulse oximetry as a teaching distractor. Oximetry percentage softened to words. DR057/DT142 test different points (appliance safety advice; pregnancy).

stem:
A 48-year-old man returns from a holiday during which he drank cheap locally made spirits. About a day later he develops vomiting, abdominal pain and blurred vision, describing his sight as 'like looking through a snowstorm'. Blood tests show a severe metabolic acidosis with a high anion gap and a raised osmolar gap. His renal function and urinalysis are normal.

Which toxin is most likely responsible?

options.A: Ethylene glycol
options.B: Isopropanol
options.C: Ethanol
options.D: Salicylate
options.E: Methanol

correct_answer: E. Methanol
why_correct: Methanol is metabolised by alcohol dehydrogenase to formic acid, which causes a high anion gap metabolic acidosis and damages the optic nerve and retina, giving the characteristic 'snowstorm' blurring; illicit or counterfeit spirits are a recognised source, and symptoms are often delayed while the toxic metabolite accumulates. Treatment is fomepizole (or ethanol) to block alcohol dehydrogenase, with haemodialysis in severe cases. Source: TOXBASE (NPIS) methanol, accessed 2026.
why_wrong: A. Ethylene glycol also causes a high anion gap acidosis and osmolar gap but characteristically leads to acute kidney injury and oxalate crystals rather than visual loss. B. Isopropanol causes drowsiness and ketosis without a significant metabolic acidosis. C. Ethanol causes intoxication but not a severe high anion gap acidosis with visual loss. D. Salicylate poisoning causes tinnitus and a mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis, without an osmolar gap or 'snowstorm' vision.
pearl: Toxic alcohol plus visual symptoms suggests methanol; toxic alcohol plus kidney injury suggests ethylene glycol.
thinking: Illicit spirits abroad  ↓  Delayed vomiting and 'snowstorm' vision  ↓  High anion gap and raised osmolar gap  ↓  Normal kidneys point away from ethylene glycol  ↓  Methanol
exam_trap: A is the trap: ethylene glycol shares the acidosis and osmolar gap, but visual disturbance belongs to methanol.
takeaway: Methanol causes a high anion gap acidosis with visual disturbance and is treated with fomepizole and dialysis.
notes: Kept Difficult by adding ethylene glycol and isopropanol as close distractors (replacing paracetamol/diazepam/carbon monoxide). NEP058 is lab-pattern led with no visual features; this is clinical recognition, not a duplicate.
